posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2015 asked What if, and the record shows how a week of questions was organized
posts.subtitle: The What if... edition read through DDW's own press releases and program, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards archive, a university exhibition brochure and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2015: What if... in the record
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2015 (What if...) from DDW releases, Dutch press, the awards archive and a university brochure, with what the record does not show.

r: A design week that picks What if... as its theme has chosen a question and not an answer, and the 2015 edition spent nine days testing how many kinds of answers a city can hold.

I like a theme that can be checked against a room. This essay reads the fourteenth edition of Dutch Design Week from published sources only: twelve press releases from DDW's own archive, the organizer's description of its history, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards gallery, an exhibition brochure from the Eindhoven University of Technology and its partners, and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview.
A short earlier version of this essay leaned on the photographs; this one starts from the documents and brings the photographs back in the second half, where they can be checked against something.

blocks.x: The numbers, and which ones to trust

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 17 to Sunday, October 25, 2015, under the theme What if...
DDW called it the fourteenth edition in several releases, and the releases for 2014 and 2016 call those years the thirteenth and the fifteenth.
That is a consistent count inside the archive of this period, so I use it.
The release of July 23 expected 2,400 participants across 80 locations.
The ticket release of late August repeated those figures.
The opening-day release raised them to 2,500 designers in almost 100 locations.

The closing release of October 25 gave the final tally under the heading "DDW in numbers": 275,000 visitors, 2,500 designers, 99 locations and 400 events, and it described the visitor number as an estimated record.
Those four numbers are the organizer's own and the release does not say how the visitor estimate was made, so I treat them as DDW's account and not as an audited count.
The comparison with the year before is in DDW's own archive. The closing release for 2014, the UP edition, reported more than 250,000 visitors, 2,400 designers, 387 events and 86 locations.

Set side by side, the 2015 figures show about 10 percent more visitors, 13 more locations and 13 more events than 2014. That arithmetic is mine, from two organizer releases, and both rest on the same kind of estimate. Omroep Brabant, writing at the start of the week, expected about 250,000 visitors, which is the 2014 figure.
The record was a surprise only in the sense that it exceeded last year's number.

blocks.x: A theme chosen to praise imagination

r: DDW's announcement said the theme celebrated the imagination of designers and called What if... the ultimate question from which creativity and innovation start.

The campaign was made with the Rotterdam design agency Fabrique, and the site was built with the Tilburg agency Freshheads; a September release says the new site grouped the program by theme and added search and design routes.

The managing director at the time, Martijn Paulen, was quoted in both the July and October releases saying that posing the right questions is the motor for the imagination, and that designers dare to question everything and shape a different answer.

It is worth reading what the theme did to the program. The releases do not use the word "answer" as a promise. They list exhibitions in which a design question is posed and left open: the Playing Life exhibitions about working with living materials, the exhibition It's Your World with its four strands (trash, health, industry, neighbor), and Thing Nothing at the Van Abbemuseum, which the July release says examines the role of design in a dematerializing world.

blocks.x: Who stood behind the week

r: Since 2009, DDW says, it has appointed two ambassadors each year to represent the week and to take part in its content.
For 2015 they were Studio Makkink & Bey, the partnership of architect Rianne Makkink and designer Jurgen Bey, and Koert van Mensvoort, the founder and director of the Next Nature Network.

The announcement says the choice of Makkink & Bey responded to growing interest in interdisciplinary working, teaching and thinking, and that Van Mensvoort's appointment fit a wish for new schools of thought on social issues.

The closing release lets the ambassadors describe the week in their own words. Makkink said that during DDW the designer becomes a curator, puts issues on the agenda and also generates new work, and she named the OXI exhibition at Sectie-C, Dutch Invertuals' work on movement, Modebelofte at the Philips Stadium and a program of football-themed content called FC DDW as examples.
Van Mensvoort said what struck him was the openness of DDW and added that the question had shifted from the world of design to the design of the world.
These are their statements as the organizer quotes them, and I report them as such.

blocks.x: One city, three areas

r: Omroep Brabant's guide to the week described the program as spread over three areas: Strijp-S, the city center between the Witte Dame and the city hall, and a group of old factories in the east of the city near the Broekakkerseweg.
DDW's own opening-week releases split the program the same way: one release for Strijp-S and one for the center.

At Strijp-S, the former Philips complex, the releases place four anchors. The Klokgebouw was open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 and held It's Your World, which DDW says was developed with support from the Stichting DOEN.

The Ketelhuisplein held the VPRO Peepshow, the CoLab Toon Design Challenge by the energy company Eneco and a collaboration between the studio HeyHeydeHaas and the designer Morag Myerscough, with music from 16:00.

The Veemgebouw, on its eighth floor, was a new DDW location that the release called a hub: the retrospective exhibition for the Dutch Design Awards finalists, In No Particular Order supported by the Creative Industries Fund NL, Hands Off: New Dutch Design at the Confluence of Technology & Craft, and three Playing Life exhibitions.

MU, the art space in the same complex, had attracted more than 35,000 visitors during DDW 2014 according to the release, and in 2015 hosted the design studio KNOL, which planned to study individual and collective behavior through spatial interventions.

In the center, the release names the Philips Stadium for Modebelofte, the Paterskerk for The Allegory of the South, the Steentjeskerk for an exhibition by Floris Hovers, the Stroomhuisje for London Calling Part 2, and the Kazerne for Open Ended by Lidewij Edelkoort.

The details are the kind that make an archive worth reading. The stadium was closed on Saturday, October 17 because of a football match, and opened at 14:00 on Sunday; the church served as a farmers' market by day, and in the evening a restaurant with a Michelin star served a set menu at a dining table more than twenty meters long.
VPRO's guide gives the price of those dinners as 150 euros including drinks, and says they were almost entirely booked.

blocks.x: What the week was arguing about

r: DDW's debates release says the program held more than 100 lectures, meetings and seminars.
It names Agatha Haines, Rachel Armstrong, Anab Jain of Superflux, Koert van Mensvoort, Stephan Petermann of OMA/AMO, Victor Knaap and Jurgen Bey among the speakers.
Three threads in that release read well next to the theme.

The first is technology and what it does to people. The third Now Future talk show, on Thursday, October 22 in the ABN AMRO House at the Klokgebouw, was hosted by Van Mensvoort, and the release says he would launch a new nature movement that evening.

The Next Nature Network release says the first ECO coin, a coin meant to express the ecological value of nature, was presented symbolically that night to Yoyo Yogasmana, who conserves more than 130 rice varieties in Indonesia without insecticides.
Yogasmana was one of the six creatives of Age of Wonderland, a four-year program curated by Arne Hendriks for Hivos and Baltan Laboratories with DDW.
The release counts what the Natlab program did in nine days: one exhibition, 21 activities, 14 guided tours and one seminar.

The second is the city. The Smart City and the Participation Society conference at the Van Abbemuseum on Friday, October 23 was set up by Het Nieuwe Instituut and the municipality of Eindhoven, who the release says had been working on that question in a multiyear program since June 1, 2015.
A Smart Board of six scientists, thinkers and designers was to be appointed there to examine the city's ambitions and formulate an action plan.

The third is the refugee crisis, which reached the Dutch news in the weeks before the week began. The release notes that VPRO would broadcast the Tegenlicht episode "Gimme shelter" on Sunday, October 18, with a meet-up on what designers could do for refugees.
The closing release says Van Mensvoort directed special attention to design in relation to the refugee issue.

Omroep Brabant's guide points to a Design Academy Eindhoven graduation project, the Limbo Embassy by Manon van Hoeckel, as a neutral meeting place meant to hold a debate without the polarization of a talk show.

blocks.x: Mind the Step and the technical universities

r: Mind the Step is the part of the edition that I can read in the most detail, because its organizers published a brochure. The Design United page says the 2015 exhibition at the Klokgebouw continued an experiment that began in 2014 as a collaboration between faculties of the Eindhoven University of Technology and Design United, the design research institute of the three technical universities of Delft, Eindhoven and Twente.
The brochure is bilingual and signed by the vice president of the TU/e executive board, Jo van Ham, by the science director of Design United, Daan van Eijk, and by Lucas Asselbergs as project leader.
It says the emphasis lay on the step the visitor can make, and the products, systems and services on show concern how people learn, move, live, stay healthy and reproduce.

Omroep Brabant names three of the exhibits: a touring motorcycle powered by electricity alone that goes around the world in 80 days, an emergency hospital that takes different shapes depending on the disaster, and a soft robotic hand that can make subtle movements.
The brochure confirms an electric motorcycle project and a soft robotics project by Rob Scharff of Delft, among its entries.
I count the brochure's entries as a program and not as a ranking of what was best.

blocks.x: Awards, and a new prize

r: The Dutch Design Awards were presented on Saturday, October 24, in the Effenaar, the first time the show was held there.

Submarine Channel won the Communication category and the Future Award for Refugee Republic, an interactive online documentary about the Domiz camp in northern Iraq, where the Dutch Design Awards entry says about 58,000 refugees lived.
The jury wrote that the team lived in the camp while working, which gives an intensity that embedded journalism does not, and that refugees were portrayed as human beings and not as victims.
Teresa van Dongen received the Young Designer Award.
The release notes that the Van Gogh Museum's multimedia tour, made by Fabrique, won the Service & Systems category, and the agency itself said so in a statement that Emerce ran as a submitted item.

For the first time the ambassadors also gave a prize for the most surprising or impressive presentation, the Best of Dutch Design Week Award. It went to Modebelofte: Performing Advancers, curated by Niek Pulles and Harm Rensink of the concept store You Are Here, praised for its presentation in an unusual place, the Philips Stadium, and for the organizers' generosity toward the fashion talent taking part.
VPRO described that show as 42 designers in six tunnels of the stadium, on a sportswear theme.

blocks.x: Tickets, music and the festival feel

r: The week also added things for visitors who came for more than the exhibitions. DDW Music, a collaboration among DDW, the Effenaar and the booking agency Friendly Fire, put daily live performances in cafes, the Van Abbemuseum, the Stroomhuis and the Ketelhuisplein, free for ticket holders.

The line-up was long, with Rufus Wainwright at the Muziekgebouw on Sunday, October 25 and Two Gallants at the Effenaar on Thursday, October 22, and The Closing Party followed the awards on Saturday, October 24.

A DDW ticket cost 16 euros online and 18.50 euros at the door, and no day tickets were sold. It gave nine days of access to the Klokgebouw, the Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show, Thing Nothing at the Van Abbemuseum and the Veemgebouw, and a 50 percent discount at the Philips Museum.
Everything else was free unless the program said otherwise.

That structure matters when reading the visitor estimate. The closing release does not say how a free-entry week with a ticketed core was counted, which is why the 275,000 figure should stay labeled as an estimate.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a collection of press photographs for 2015 with 45 albums, and the account's pages say the images may be published for non-commercial purposes with the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week stated.
I opened six of the 45 albums on October 9, 2026, covering 191 photographs by the counts on the pages, and I did not return to them for this version.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 33 photographs by Cleo Goossens, Tommy Köhlbrugge and Almicheal Fraay. A high view by Goossens looks across the square in autumn, with yellow trees in the foreground, white tents and a stage, and two red and white chimneys behind. A photograph by Köhlbrugge shows a tower of scaffolding hung with colored panels and letters, one of them a large question mark. The releases do not name a tower, so I use the picture for its question mark and nothing more. A third photograph shows a bulb-lit stand for the VPRO Peepshow, which the October 17 release places on the Ketelhuisplein.

The Klokgebouw album holds 50 photographs by Sjoerd Eickmans, titled Klokgebouw_div with a number. One shows black and white patterned fabric on a mannequin and a sign reading Zeeuws Museum Handwerk; I can say whose stand it is and not who designed the print. A separate album, 3TU & TU/e: Mind the Step, holds 31 photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann, including a mannequin torso in a dark purple shirt with a strip of small circuit boards stitched down the middle. The brochure and the album fit the same exhibition, and no caption says what those circuits do.

The Kazerne Expo album holds 30 photographs by Ralph Roelse. An earlier draft said no release named the Kazerne. That was wrong: the October 15 release names the Kazerne for Open Ended by Lidewij Edelkoort, and the July release lists it among the hot spots.

The album shows a dark gallery with a brick wall, a red glazed bowl on a white plinth, and a red wool coat on a mannequin arm. I still cannot say which of the Kazerne's exhibitions the coat belongs to, because the photo title carries only the venue.

The MU album, titled Collective [Ir]Rationality, holds 18 photographs by Köhlbrugge and Daan Paans, one of them of visitors walking beside a pale factory wall toward an entrance marked by white posts and an orange barrier.

An earlier draft said the October 17 release lists Playing Life exhibitions at MU. That was also wrong. The release puts the three Playing Life exhibitions in the Veemgebouw and describes MU's program separately, as the work of the studio KNOL, which fits the album's title about collective behavior.

The Sectie-C album holds 49 photographs, among them Iris Rijskamp's pictures titled 91_OXI. One shows a glass case on a dark table, and another a case holding a gray bird hung on wires next to a printed card reading OXI and SALUTES.

The earlier draft said it did not know what OXI is. The record now answers that. The closing release names OXI on Sectie-C as an exhibition by Justine Kontou, Tessa Koot and Club-C, and Makkink described it as a challenge to the revenue model for designers.

VPRO adds that OXI's curator was Kontou, that one work, Dadabase by Govert Flint, scanned a visitor's face to recognize age, gender and emotion as a way to produce data that has value, and that Sectie-C was home to 180 creative entrepreneurs, craftspeople and artists opening their studios.
The card and the case in the photograph are consistent with that description. They do not tell me which object is Flint's.

blocks.x: A visit from parliament

r: On Monday, October 19, a delegation of members of parliament from the standing committees for Economic Affairs and for Education, Culture and Science made a working visit to the creative industry at DDW.

The Dutch release says the mayor of Eindhoven, Rob van Gijzel, the chair of the Dutch Creative Council, Jeroen van Erp, and Martijn Paulen presented their view on the importance of the creative industry for the Netherlands and for Brainport Eindhoven, and that the members saw research and design projects by the three technical universities and the Graduation Show of the Design Academy Eindhoven.
The release gives the festival's standing scale as more than 2,400 designers presenting to some 260,000 visitors a year, more than 400 events and 100 locations.
That 260,000 sits between the 250,000-plus of 2014 and the 275,000 of 2015, and it is a description of a typical year, not a count.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The July release expected 2,400 participants in 80 locations, and the closing release reports 2,500 designers in 99 locations. The closing release is later and says it is a tally, so I use it.
Omroep Brabant wrote that the week began on a Friday evening, while DDW's releases give Saturday, October 17 as the first day and say, on that date, that the week gets underway "today".
DDW's own dates settle the program days. The Friday evening report may describe an opening event, which the sources I opened do not describe.
The earlier draft placed it at MU. DDW's October 17 release places it in the Veemgebouw.
Both were unexplained in the earlier draft and both are named in DDW releases.
The archive's own releases agree on the fourteenth, the thirteenth and the fifteenth for 2015, 2014 and 2016.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how DDW produced the visitor estimate, and neither the July nor the October releases explain it.
I do not know which of the roughly 100 locations received the most visitors. The only per-venue figure in the sources is MU's 35,000 visitors in 2014, from the opening release.
I cannot say what the 39 Flickr albums I did not open show, or whether other photographers recorded exhibits I did not read about.

I do not have a complete list of Dutch Design Awards winners for 2015 from a primary page. The gallery entry I opened covers Refugee Republic, and the other winners I name come from DDW's closing release and one submitted press item.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If you look at the 2015 archive this month, pick one room and ask the question the theme asked: what if the thing in that photograph had been designed for a different person, and who would that person be?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2016 was about the making of things, and the record shows who paid for the making
posts.subtitle: The fifteenth edition read through DDW's press archive, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards gallery, a municipal quote, a state funding announcement and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2016: The making of, in the record
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2016 (The making of) from DDW releases, Dutch press, the awards gallery and the official photo archive, with the funding and what is unknown.

r: A festival that names its theme The making of is promising to show how things get made, and in 2016 the record shows that the festival itself was being made at the same time, with new money, a new network and a new prize.

I like a theme that can be checked against a workshop. This essay reads the fifteenth edition of Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten press releases from DDW's archive, two of them in Dutch, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards gallery, a listing from the Waag research institute and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft of this essay used three releases and the photographs. This version adds the program, the awards, the funding and the people, and it corrects what the earlier draft could not name.

blocks.x: The numbers

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 22 to Sunday, October 30, 2016, under the theme The making of.
The announcement of July 21 expected 2,500 designers across 100 locations.
The closing release of October 30 reported an estimated record of 295,000 visitors, 2,500 designers and more than 430 curated exhibitions and presentations across 100 locations.
A year earlier DDW had reported 275,000 visitors, 2,500 designers, 99 locations and 400 events.

Set side by side, the 2016 visitor figure is about 7 percent higher, and the count of exhibitions and presentations is about 7 percent higher if the 2015 "events" and the 2016 "curated exhibitions and presentations" mean the same thing, which neither release says. Both visitor numbers are estimates by DDW's own description, and no release explains the method.
One number needs a caution. The release about Queen Máxima's visit, dated October 25, says DDW had "more than 275,000 visitors", and a Waag listing for its own events uses the same figure.
Both repeat the previous year's total as the standing description of the event. The 295,000 estimate is the one the closing release gives for 2016.

blocks.x: A theme about alienation

r: DDW's announcement said the theme puts the making process center stage, honors the makers and tackles alienation by revealing how everyday products and services are made, or where.
The managing director at the time, Martijn Paulen, said Dutch designers are critical and enterprising, make a lot themselves and also tackle social issues.
The campaign came from the agency Fabrique, whose creative director André Bouwman described it as an ode to the making process and the makers.

The anniversary framed the program too. The announcement named the Graduation Show of the Design Academy Eindhoven, the Dutch Design Awards, the Dutch Invertuals show and Modebelofte as regular highlights, and listed the Designhuis, the Van Abbemuseum, Kazerne, MU, the Creative Industries Fund NL, Piet Hein Eek, Sectie-C, TAC and Yksi as sites of international exhibitions.

In the Klokgebouw, under the art direction of Overtreders W, it placed It's Your World, made with ambassador Bas van Abel, and Mind the Step by the technical universities of Delft, Twente and Eindhoven.

blocks.x: Two ambassadors and a royal visit

r: DDW announced Maarten Baas and Bas van Abel as the 2016 ambassadors on February 16, 2016, and said it has named two ambassadors a year since 2009.
Baas is an autonomous designer whose work sits between art and design.
Van Abel had founded Fairphone in 2013 and received a Momentum for Change Award from UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon in 2016, according to the announcement.

Van Abel's exhibition in the Klokgebouw was called The Making of Your World. DDW's release describes it as a response to consumers losing their grasp of the complex world behind everyday products, and it says Van Abel developed a sustainable telephone himself and asks in the exhibition how product development can balance economic and other values.
Waag's listing says the guiding principles were Van Abel's experiences with making that telephone, and it lists a Waag do-it-yourself finger splint among the exhibits.
Waag's listing gives the Veemgebouw as the location for its own program. DDW's July and October releases place The Making of Your World in the Klokgebouw, and I use that.

On Tuesday, October 25, Queen Máxima visited. DDW's release says she looked at The Making of Your World and Mind the Step, spoke with designers on the Ketelhuisplein, and talked with a group that included Baas, Jeroen van Erp, Thomas Widdershoven, Dave Hakkens and Christien Meindertsma about the status of Dutch design.

The release defines Dutch design as an attitude and not only a nationality, and it describes a hybrid practice in which product design, graphic design, landscape design, architecture and gaming are hard to tell apart.
That is DDW's framing of a royal conversation, and the release is the only source I opened for it.

blocks.x: Time, made in a garage

r: For the anniversary Baas curated Maarten Baas Makes Time, which ran from October 22 to 30 in the former Van der Meulen Ansems garage at Vestdijk 25/27 in the center of Eindhoven.

The August 31 release calls it a mix of design, visual art, performing arts and gastronomy. The heart of the show was work by Atelier NL, Jurgen Bey, Joost van Bleiswijk and Kiki van Eijk, realized with the theater maker Joris van Midde of De Kwekerij. The textile maker Vlisco, the ceramics producer Cor Unum and VPRO were partners. Baas also showed a preview of his book Hide & Seek and new work for the Carpenters Workshop Gallery.
In a temporary restaurant designed by Baas, the chef Sergio Herman served a menu of his signature dishes.

The site was made available by the municipality of Eindhoven, and the alderman for work, economy and vocational training, Staf Depla, was quoted calling it a good example of the added value of the city's acquisition team, which brought parties together early to create an event that draws more people to the city center.
The exhibition could only be visited with a DDW ticket, at 17.50 euros online before service costs.
The release does not say how many people attended, and the closing release does not either.

blocks.x: Bamboo, a square and a party each night

r: The Ketelhuisplein had been rebuilt for the week. The closing release names "the transformation of the Ketelhuisplein with Bambooh Lala" among the highlights that visitors, designers and media partners were enthusiastic about.

A preview listing explains what that was: the creative agency HeyHeydeHaas designed a "never finished" bamboo construction meant to connect everything and everyone on the square, with a bar called the Inwisselbar at its center hosting a different party each evening between 17:00 and 20:00.
The same agency had worked with the designer Morag Myerscough on the square a year earlier.
I can therefore name the builder of the bamboo scaffolds that the earlier draft of this essay could only describe. The earlier draft said no source named who built it.

blocks.x: A program that argued about bodies, homes and phones

r: Several things on the program show how wide the theme stretched. At MU, For Play, Shaping Sexuality showed 37 works by 34 designers, according to VPRO, and the preview listing names the co-curators as Sanne Muiser and Tom Loois and says more than 30 artists and designers contributed.

The two counts are compatible, since one counts works and the other people. A Home Away From Home was a competition by the Dutch Central Agency for the Reception of Asylum Seekers and the Government Architect, Floris Alkemade, to design better housing for refugees, and its six winners were shown during the week; one, the Solar Cabin by Bram Zondag and Arjan de Nooijer, was being built on the Stadhuisplein, VPRO wrote.
Sectie-C, the former factory ground in Tongelre, was the place where VPRO said the theme fit like a glove, because visitors walked into the designers' workshops.
In hall 6 the group Collaboration O housed 13 designers.

Modebelofte had moved from the Philips Stadium, where it showed in 2015, to the roof of the department store De Bijenkorf, with the theme Adaptive Travelers and about 30 recently graduated fashion talents.
Dutch Invertuals presented Power Play for the fifteenth time, an exploration of the aesthetics of energy overload curated by Wendy Plomp, at the NS Loods.
IKEA showed the STUNSIG collection with the duo Pinar&Viola in the Klokgebouw.

The Graduation Show of the Design Academy Eindhoven filled three floors, VPRO wrote, and its chair Jurriënne Ossewold said the students were activists on gender, refugees, privacy and the environment.
Age of Wonderland, in its third year, took big and open data as its subject, with fellows from Chile, Guatemala, Indonesia, Iran and Tanzania and a seminar on Monday, October 24 at Natlab.
The program was run by Hivos, Baltan Laboratories and the Dutch Design Foundation.

blocks.x: The Kazerne and ESCAPE

r: The Kazerne is a monumental exhibition space with a restaurant, and its own website lists the exhibition ESCAPE under 2016 to 2017 for the designer group BCXSY, with a work called Light Forest.
The earlier draft said it could not say what the work was for. The Kazerne's page gives the title and one work, and I still cannot say which glass objects in the photographs belong to which exhibit.

blocks.x: Awards and a new prize

r: The Dutch Design Awards were presented on Saturday, October 29.
Christien Meindertsma won the Product category and the Future Award for her FLAX Chair, made with Label Breed and Enkev from flax fiber and polylactide.
The jury wrote that she had researched flax for years and had even bought a plot to learn how it can be processed, and that the project was more than another chair.

Tom van Soest received the Young Designer Award, Brabantia the award for the best commissioner, and Crystal Houses by MVRDV, a load-bearing glass brick developed with TU Delft, ABT and Poesia, the Public Award.
The Dutch Design Awards gallery lists the glass brick as a 2016 winner in the Product category as well, which the release does not mention, so I do not know whether it won in both.

For the second year DDW gave a Best of Dutch Design Week prize. A panel of seven designers and visitors compiled a shortlist of 16 projects, and on Sunday, October 30 the ambassadors gave an encouragement prize to Forest Wool by Tamara Orjola of the Design Academy Eindhoven, with 2,500 euros from a private donor and a presentation place in the next edition.

blocks.x: Money, networks and a next step

r: The edition also shows how DDW's institutional footing was changing. On September 20, the government's budget papers for 2017 included the Cultuurnota 2017 to 2020 with 10 million euros extra for culture, and DDW was named among those who would receive support: 400,000 euros a year from the education, culture and science budget for 2017 to 2020.
Paulen called it recognition of the week as a national platform.

In the same weeks DDW hosted the official launch of the World Design Weeks Network on October 22 at Piet Hein Eek, where nine promoters, among them design weeks from Barcelona, Beijing, Helsinki, Mexico, San Francisco, Seoul, Tokyo and Toronto together with the Dutch Design Foundation, signed the incorporation documents.
The release says 35 parties had registered for membership and the head office is in Helsinki.

On Monday, October 24, at the Van Abbemuseum, the theme year Mondriaan to Dutch design 2017 was kicked off, and with it a plan for a World Design Event in Eindhoven parallel to DDW in 2017, with 500 volunteers building a People's Pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein that summer, and a goal of 400,000 visitors for the event together with the design week.

Alongside this, DDW and the crowdfunding site Kickstarter launched what the closing release calls the first crowdfunding page for Dutch design, with campaigns for 11 projects shown in a retrospective in the Kazerne, and the city's first alderman of design, Mary-Ann Schreurs, secured a dyslexia font by Christian Boer for the schools and residents of Eindhoven at the final auction.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2016 collection of press photographs with 46 albums, and the account's pages say the images may be published for non-commercial purposes if the photographer and Dutch Design Week are named.
I opened five of the 46 on October 9, 2026 and a sixth that I did not use, and I did not return to them for this version.

The VDMA album holds 30 photographs by Nick Bookelaar, each titled VDMA. One shows a hall with a pale wire-frame walking sculpture lit from below, with its shadow cast across a floor of red and white cell patterns. Another shows a place setting from above on a red and orange wax-print cloth, with a plate arranged into a smiling face. A third shows a dark dining hall hung with flags and glass. Wax-print cloth fits the release's naming of Vlisco as a partner, and the place settings fit a show with a chef, but I cannot say which designer made which object.

The Klokgebouw album holds 48 photographs by Cleo Goossens, eight of them titled Mind the Step. I used none of those, because each shows visitors in close view or a dense crowd that includes young people. One photograph looks down on a shelf of speckled plates, cups and notebooks, titled Frameshop.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 67 photographs, and the titles include ABN AMRO, Bamboe and Banners. A high view by Goossens shows pale bamboo structures, bicycles in racks and autumn trees. The photograph titled Banners shows a black banner on a white building reading THE MAKING OF and PERSISTENCE IS FRUITFUL, with the dates 22 to 30 October. The dates match the release. The slogan appears in no release I read, so I report the words and nothing about who chose them.

The Kazerne album holds 54 photographs by Ralph Roelse, titled ESCAPE and ESCAPE DRIFT, and the Sectie-C album holds 112 photographs by Iris Rijskamp, titled with file numbers. The Kazerne photographs show glass tube lights, a high black hall hung with glass bulbs and a wooden tray of colored pegs. The Sectie-C photographs include hanging clay-colored forms and a skull made of golden fragments on a steel stand.

blocks.x: Music as a measured part of the week

r: The two DDW Music releases give 2016 a number that the closing release does not. DDW Music, organized with the Effenaar and the booking agency Friendly Fire, was said to have attracted over 5,000 visitors in 2015, and for 2016 the second edition planned performances by more than 60 artists in 12 locations from October 22 to 30.

The venues included the Effenaar, Nul Zes, Gaslab, Fifth NRE, the Van Abbemuseum, Stroomhuis, Altstadt, the Old Courthouse, Cafe Wilhelmina, the Muziekgebouw and Calypso, and the Ketelhuisplein hosted a DDW Music Lab by the composers Strijbos & van Rijswijk, open daily from 12:00 to 18:00 with free entry funded by the Effenaar Poplab.
A go-as-you-please ticket cost 17.50 euros before service charges, and a concert without it 5 euros at the door.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: 275,000 appears in the Máxima release and in Waag's text; 295,000 in the closing release. The closing release is the later and more specific document, and the other two repeat the previous year's number.
Where The Making of Your World was.
Waag's location field says the Veemgebouw, DDW's releases say the Klokgebouw. DDW's own words settle the exhibition's place, and Waag's field probably describes its own booth.
DDW says the glass brick took the Public Award, and the awards gallery lists it as a Product winner. I cannot settle that from what I opened.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how DDW produced the 295,000 estimate, or how many people saw Maarten Baas Makes Time.
I do not know which of the Kazerne's exhibits the glass bulbs and tubes belong to, or who curated ESCAPE.
The Dutch Design Awards gallery entries I opened cover two winners, so the full list of 2016 winners is not in this essay.
I did not open the 41 Flickr albums I skipped, and I did not re-read the five I used.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If you read a festival's archive for money before you read it for objects, whose making do you expect to find paid for in the photographs, and whose do you expect to find missing?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2017 stretched, and the record shows a second festival built into the first
posts.subtitle: The Stretch edition read through DDW's press archive, the World Design Event, the Dutch Design Awards, Dutch press and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2017: Stretch, in the record
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2017 (Stretch) from DDW releases, the World Design Event, the awards, a spending survey and the photo archive, with what is not known.

r: A theme called Stretch promises that things get pulled past their usual limits, and in 2017 the organizer pulled its own event past its limits by adding a second festival, a borrowed pavilion and a third ambassador.

I like a theme that can be tested against its structure. This essay reads the sixteenth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: fifteen items from DDW's press archive, trade-press reports on the awards and on a visitor and spending survey, a materials site on the pavilion, the exhibition pages of the technical universities and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft relied on three releases and the photographs, and some of its statements change below.

blocks.x: The numbers, and what they count

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 21 to Sunday, October 29, 2017.

DDW's closing release reported "more than 335,000 visitors" for Dutch Design Week and the World Design Event together, 2,600 designers, 610 exhibitions, presentations, tours and activities, and 110 locations.
The earlier draft of this essay read the 335,000 as the count for DDW alone. The release's first sentence says otherwise: the figure belongs to the two events combined.
A music release written the same week does describe 335,000 as the visitors to Dutch Design Week, so DDW itself uses the number both ways.
The trade site IO+ quoted DDW's head of brand strategy as saying the growth was partly caused by the World Design Event, and it reported that the share of foreign visitors rose from 12 to 18 percent.
A year later the same site reported 355,000 visitors for 2018 and DDW's director saying that the growth could not be put down to the World Design Event, because it had continued without it.
I report 335,000 as the organizer's combined figure.
The year before, DDW had reported 295,000 visitors, 2,500 designers, more than 430 curated exhibitions and presentations and 100 locations.

Visitors rose about 14 percent, designers by 100 and locations by 10. The count of events rose from 430 to 610, but the 2017 count includes tours and activities and the 2016 count says "curated exhibitions and presentations", so I do not compare them.
When DDW announced the World Design Event in October 2016, it set a goal of 400,000 visitors for the new event and the design week together.
The closing figure is about 84 percent of that goal. Neither the 2016 plan nor the 2017 release says how visitors were counted.

blocks.x: A theme that asked people to leave their comfort zone

r: The announcement of the theme, on July 27, said the organizer wanted participants and the public to dare to break out of their comfort zone.
Martijn Paulen, the director, called Dutch design yoga for the brain.
The campaign, again by Fabrique, was built with 15 designers who transformed existing work into new forms, according to Fabrique's creative director André Bouwman.
The release also notes that DDW began choosing a theme for the week in 2012.
The About DDW page lists the themes since then, from Enter a Brave New World in 2012 to Stretch in 2017.
Paulen's closing statement picked the same verb up: designers like working together, look for the edges of possibility and stretch, as professional idealists.
That is a director describing his own week, and I treat it as the organizer's framing.

blocks.x: Three ambassadors, the first of them international

r: The ambassadors were announced on June 30. Where DDW had named two a year since 2009, in 2017 it named three: the architect Winy Maas of MVRDV, the designers Lonny van Ryswyck and Nadine Sterk of Atelier NL, and Marcus Fairs, founder and editor-in-chief of the design magazine Dezeen.
DDW said the change was meant to underpin the international character of the ambassadorship and called Fairs its first international ambassador.
Atelier NL planned a new interactive project, To See a World in a Grain of Sand.
In the closing release Maas said the ambassadorship does not end with the week and gives him homework to follow up with designers, organizations and ministries.
Fairs said Dutch Design Week is a kind of laboratory for design that could save the world.
Those are their words as quoted by the organizer.

blocks.x: What the program said it was about

r: The complete program was published on September 27. It listed more than 600 exhibitions, presentations, lectures and network meetings and named its trends: digitalization and robotization, social issues and the circular economy, and a special role for crafts, meaning the rediscovery of old methods and new applications for them.

New locations included Core Studio at Q-Park Emmasingel, the Embassy of Robot Love and the Embassy of Data in the former V&D department store, the Embassy of Health on Strijp T, HUBOT by the Next Nature Network at the MediaMarkt, Contemplation Spaces in the Student Hotel, and the exhibition Young Collectors in Woensel-West.

The release also tells readers where the regulars stood. Many exhibitions were in the VEEM and on the Ketelhuisplein in Strijp-S, in the VDMA building and on the NRE terrain, and the Klokgebouw, under the art direction of Overtreders W, accommodated Mind the Step.
The Van Abbemuseum, Kazerne, MU, Piet Hein Eek, Sectie-C, ABN AMRO, the Textile Museum and TAC again organized exhibitions.

The closing release names the Van Abbemuseum exhibition Beyond Generations among the year's highlights, and the program release lists MU's Materialising the Internet under the trend it calls the immaterial materialized.

blocks.x: The World Design Event and a pavilion made of loans

r: DDW's October 24, 2016 announcement had introduced the World Design Event as a four-yearly event parallel to DDW, with 500 volunteers building a People's Pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein.

The closing release reports that the first edition was well attended, helped by Marcus Fairs's talk Good Design for a Bad World, by Antenna, a showcase of young designers made with Design Indaba, and by seven Embassies of the Future.
The program release gave the event eight challenges: food, health, urban development, data, climate, intimacy, robotization, and mobility and energy.

The People's Pavilion was designed by Overtreders W and Bureau SLA. DDW's release says it was made from 100 percent borrowed materials, lent by suppliers, manufacturers and Eindhoven residents, and to be returned intact after nine days.
The walls and frames came from the Urban Mining Collective of the company New Horizon, a group the release lists with partners that include ABN AMRO, Knauf, Rexel and Wavin.

MaterialDistrict adds that no glue, screws, drills or saws were used, and that 9,500 shingles for the facade were made from plastic waste supplied by residents, each fixed with two cable ties, which is why the trade site says the building was not completely waste free.

The organizer's phrase "100% circular" and the trade site's caveat can both stand: the loans were returned, and the cable ties were not borrowed. The closing release says the pavilion hosted more than 50 events.

The same release set a larger intention: New Horizon and DDW said they aimed to recover all material needed for DDW and its participants through urban mining in the following year, so as to make a circular DDW.
I do not know whether that was achieved.

blocks.x: Other threads in the week

r: The railway company NS and DDW's What if Lab had four design concepts tested by passengers on trains to Eindhoven during the week: a quiz game, a mindfulness coaching app, moving furniture and an audio tour, designed respectively by Waarmakers, Studio Jan Pieter Kaptein, Enrichers and Manon van Hoeckel with Tom Loois.
NS also showed a mock-up of a "train of tomorrow" on the Ketelhuisplein.
Crowdfunding Dutch Design returned for a second edition with twelve projects, shown in the Klokgebouw and funded through Kickstarter and the Dutch platform Voordekunst.
The twelve included a sleep robot, a hybrid chair and a collection of cutlery.

VPRO and DDW, which had worked together as content partners for five years, launched the television series De toekomstbouwers, in which eight emerging designers took part and one received a grant of 10,000 euros; the candidates included Frank Kolkman and Bas Timmer.
IO+ reports that Dave Hakkens won it with Precious Plastic, and it gives the series a slightly different title, Toekomstmakers; I use the title in DDW's release.
DDW Music, in its third edition, put on more than 70 artists, drew more than 16,000 visitors and sold out three quarters of its performances, according to a joint release by DDW and the Effenaar.
A DDW ticket cost 19 euros online including service costs, and a concert without it cost 5 euros.

blocks.x: Awards

r: The Dutch Design Awards were presented on Saturday, October 28.
DeFlat Kleiburg by NL Architects and XVW architectuur, the renovation of an apartment block in the Bijlmermeer, won the Future Award.

The category winners were Vlisco Un à Un by Michiel Schuurman for Communication, ZandGlas by Atelier NL for Design Research, Bravado by Das Leben am Haverkamp for Fashion, Quooker Flex for Product and White Spots by Studio Richard Vijgen for Service & Systems.
Frank Kolkman received the Young Designer Award for his speculative work on care, including Open Surgery and Designs for Flies.
Royal FloraHolland won the prize for commissioning for its work with Vandejong on the Let it Grow brand.
Sheltersuit 4.0 by Bas Timmer had the most public votes and won the Public Award.
The jury included Deyan Sudjic of the Design Museum London and Rosa Bertoli of Wallpaper.
DeFlat Kleiburg's entry in the awards gallery explains the prize: only the main structure was modernized, and the future residents decide how to finish the apartments.
The committee called it a noteworthy achievement given that it was developed at the height of the financial crisis.

blocks.x: What the week meant for the city

r: A survey commissioned by DDW and run by the research agency Dynamic Concepts, with more than 1,200 visitors, estimated that the 335,000 visitors spent almost 15 million euros in shops and hospitality, more than a third of it in hospitality, and that the event sustained 108 jobs in tourism.
Visitors rated the quality of the program 7.9 and the quality of exhibitions and projects 8, while the lectures, debates, music and design routes scored lower, around 7.3.
The survey put the media value of DDW at 17 million euros by an international standard that measures how far media pick an event up.

Paulen said the economic effect was a side effect for the organization, whose first concern was whether designers had a good week, and that the benefit to participants is hard to measure because DDW is not a trade fair.
The figures are the commissioning organization's, quoted by a trade site, and I have not seen the report.
DDW's funding was changing in the same period. The state had announced 400,000 euros a year for DDW for 2017 to 2020 in September 2016.

blocks.x: Mind the Step in the record

r: DDW's program releases name Mind the Step among the Klokgebouw's exhibitions in 2017.
Design United's pages for the exhibition list editions for 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2018, followed by a different title for 2019, and none for 2017.
The gap does not contradict DDW, since the Design United list may omit a year or fold it into a neighboring one, and I cannot tell which. For 2017 I rely on the DDW statement alone.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2017 collection with 67 albums, and its pages say photographers' names and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened six of the 67 on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.

The Klokgebouw album holds 26 photographs by Cleo Goossens and Ruud Balk. One shows a bright hall with a yellow counter and stands headed Climate change impact, where a person in a red suit walks between panels. The program places Mind the Step in the Klokgebouw, and I cannot say whether the yellow hall belongs to it.

The VEEM album holds 113 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 24, 2017, and the titles are sorted by school: Bauhaus Universität, Burg Giebichenstein, Central Saint Martins and ECAL. The earlier draft could not say why. The closing release answers: it lists among the educational presentations those of ECAL in Lausanne, the Bauhaus Universität Weimar, the Burg Giebichenstein university in Halle and Central Saint Martins.

I chose a close view of a textile that looks like a mat of pale threads, from the Bauhaus group, and a close view of black stone and silver pendants from the Central Saint Martins group. The titles name the school and not the student, so I do not call the textile any material.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 38 photographs, mostly by Goossens, and the titles name ABN Amro. One shows a tall green house-shaped box with small holes and a yellow key on its roof. ABN AMRO is named in the program among the exhibitors and in the closing release for Driving Dutch Design and Hotspots, and I cannot tie the green box to either.

The Van Abbemuseum album, titled Beyond Generations, holds 26 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge. The Kazerne album holds 16 photographs by Ralph Roelse, and the MU album 32 photographs by Kneefel titled Materialising the Internet, which the program names as a trend example.

blocks.x: Four talks, a symposium and a pavilion that kept winning

r: The week's talks were a headline in their own right. Dezeen, which DDW's music release names as a media partner, teamed with DDW to launch Good Design for a Bad World, five panel discussions over the weekend of October 21 and 22, on climate change, refugees, terrorism, pollution and politics, as ambassador Marcus Fairs's contribution.
Confirmed speakers included the humanitarian expert Kilian Kleinschmidt, the architect Winy Maas, the designer Dave Hakkens and the What Design Can Do organizer Richard van der Laken.
The page is DDW's repost of Dezeen's announcement, and I did not open Dezeen itself.

The MU exhibition Materialising the Internet, which the earlier draft saw only as a title in an album, is described by DDW's trend page as an example of making the immaterial physical: it argues that the virtual is already integrated in our environment, with algorithms that link you to a new love, GIFs stored in DNA and RFID chips implanted in hands, and it features Lauren McCarthy's work on smart devices that register everything.

A symposium, The Abundance and Scarcity of Sand, hosted by Atelier NL and MU on the disappearing resource, had a keynote by the filmmaker Denis Delestrac and a panel including Winy Maas, Lonny van Ryswyck and Marcus Fairs, tickets 10 euros.
DDW also reposted a note from Agri meets Design reflecting on the 2017 Embassy of Food.

The People's Pavilion kept collecting recognition after the week. DDW announced that it won the first Frame Sustainability Award, from the jury of the Frame Awards, and the Dutch Design Awards later listed it as a 2018 winner in the Habitat category.
The Frame page gives the awards show as February 21 and a link text dated 2017, which cannot be right for a pavilion built in October 2017, so I read it as February 2018.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The closing release says DDW and the World Design Event together. A music release says DDW. The closing release is the primary account of the count, so I use "combined".
DDW says 100 percent borrowed and circular. MaterialDistrict says cable ties mean it was not waste free. Both are consistent with a borrowed structure and plastic shingles.
DDW names it. Design United's edition list has no 2017 entry. Unresolved.
Whether the record was the World Design Event's doing.

DDW credits the new event with part of the growth in 2017, and a year later its director said the growth continued without it. Both statements can hold: the combined figure rose 14 percent, and the design week alone then grew another 6 percent in 2018 according to IO+.
Why the VEEM titles are schools.
The closing release names the schools as educational presentations.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how 335,000 was counted, or how many of those visitors came for the World Design Event alone.
I do not know whether the circular DDW that New Horizon and DDW proposed for 2018 was achieved.
I do not know which exhibition the yellow Klokgebouw hall or the green ABN AMRO box belongs to.
I did not read the 61 albums I skipped.
I have not seen the Dynamic Concepts survey itself, so its sample, its method and the definition of visitor spending are not known to me.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival adds a second festival, which of the two do you think a visitor in the photographs would have counted as the main one?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2018 asked who else would do it, and the record shows who showed up
posts.subtitle: The If not us, then who? edition read through DDW's releases, the Dutch Design Awards, the technical universities' exhibition pages, Kazerne's own account and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2018: If not us, then who?
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2018 (If not us, then who?) from DDW releases, the Dutch Design Awards, the university exhibitions, Kazerne and the photo archive.

r: A theme phrased as a question about who should act has to be answered by someone, and in 2018 the people it named were designers, a car maker, a university and a restaurant that was also a museum.

I like a theme that names its own audience. This essay reads the seventeenth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: seven items from DDW's press archive, the Dutch Design Awards' own announcement, two university and exhibition pages, Kazerne's website, trade-press reports on attendance and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases, one wire item and the photographs, and several of its open questions have answers below.

blocks.x: The numbers, and the growth that needed explaining

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 20 to Sunday, October 28, 2018, under the theme If not us, then who?
The closing release reported 355,000 visitors, 2,600 designers, 499 exhibitions, lectures, tours and labs, and 120 locations.
It describes the visitors as professionals, industry representatives, governments, visitors and journalists, so the count mixes audiences and is not a ticket count.

The year before, DDW had reported more than 335,000 visitors, 2,600 designers, 610 exhibitions, presentations, tours and activities, and 110 locations, but that count covered Dutch Design Week and the World Design Event together.
Omroep Brabant, reporting the 2017 close, wrote that the 335,000 was 40,000 more than the year before.

That makes 2018 a growth of about 6 percent in visitors, 10 more locations and 111 fewer events, and the event count is not comparable because the 2017 figure includes tours and activities and a second festival.
The trade site IO+ reported the 6 percent and quoted DDW's director Martijn Paulen on an increase of 21 percent in international visitors.
IO+ also wrote that the previous record had been attributed to the World Design Event, and that the 2018 result showed DDW growing on its own strength.
That is a reading by the reporter and the organizer, and no source I opened breaks the 2017 figure into its two events.
An earlier IO+ item about 2017 gave the share of foreign visitors as rising from 12 to 18 percent.
No 2018 share is given in the sources I opened, only the 21 percent increase, so I cannot say what percentage of visitors came from abroad in 2018.

blocks.x: A tribute written as a question

r: The theme was announced on September 5, with just under seven weeks to go.

Paulen's text says that almost everything in the world has been or is being designed, which brings opportunities and enormous responsibilities for designers but also for policy makers, commissioners, users and governments, and that designers continually supply authentic and surprising answers to "how could it be different, better?"
The closing release calls the theme a tribute to designers.

The same announcement launched a new website built with the digital agency Vruchtvlees of The Hague, which DDW described as a content platform that would run all year with articles, interviews, videos and podcasts.
It introduced a choice of four ticket types: festival, basic, premium and professional.
DDW Music Festival was announced with more than 90 artists, from a pianist at Piet Hein Eek to Thai funk at the Effenaar.

blocks.x: Three ambassadors from three worlds

r: The ambassadors, announced on June 22, were Ravi Naidoo, founder of Design Indaba in South Africa, Laurens van den Acker, senior vice president of corporate design at Renault, and Wendy Plomp of Dutch Invertuals.

Paulen tied each to a value of the organization: Naidoo to talent development, inclusivity and internationalization, Van den Acker to the link between people, innovation, technology, mobility and industry, Plomp to innovation, research and experiment.
Naidoo and DDW had introduced a platform called Antenna together the year before.

The release lists the three ambassador quotes as "We bring our trademark activism to DDW" from Naidoo, "A virtuoso soloist is often supported by a great symphony orchestra" from Van den Acker, and "Companies and institutions are increasingly embracing creative spirits" from Plomp.
The fact that a car company's design chief served as an ambassador connects to the next item.

DDW and Renault announced a partnership on March 30: 45 fully electric Renault ZOE cars would serve as Design Rides, the free shuttles that carry visitors between locations, for the first time electric.
The release says Design Rides had been a regular part of the program for many years and one of the most photographed projects of the festival.
Renault's Dutch spokesperson called DDW an excellent stage for the brand, and said the brand's Dutch design chief, Van den Acker, had made design the first reason customers buy.
That sentence is a company's statement about itself, and I report it as such.

blocks.x: The universities in the Klokgebouw

r: The Klokgebouw at Strijp-S held two exhibitions by the technical universities in 2018.

Mind the Step, from Design United, ran from October 20 to 28 in the Klokgebouw and organized its projects under six themes: Design for Debate, Health and Wellbeing, Home and Leisure, Improving Professional Environments, Innovative Materials and The New Mobility, the last subtitled "Clean, safe, and fast forward".
The steering committee included the vice president of the TU/e executive board and the project leader was Lucas Asselbergs.
Beside it stood the first exhibition made by the Eindhoven University of Technology itself at DDW, TU/e Research, with the subtitle Drivers of Change.
Its four focus areas were looking inside the body, the house as an energy supplier, the internet of the future and safe driving, with two research projects in each.

Asselbergs, who advised on it, said the university had taken part in DDW since 2002 but mostly through industrial design and architecture, and he estimated 100,000 of the 2017 visitors had come to the Klokgebouw.
That estimate is his and covers 2017.

These two pages let me correct the earlier draft's reading of the photographs. A high view of a Klokgebouw hall shows banners spelling STEP and a panel headed Clean, safe and fast forward. That heading is Mind the Step's mobility theme. A second photograph with panels in Dutch headed Het huis als energieleverancier and Internet van de toekomst belongs to TU/e Research. The earlier draft read the panel headings against a single wire item. The two pages show that the first heading belongs to Mind the Step and the second to TU/e Research, two neighboring exhibitions.

blocks.x: Kazerne becomes a home of design

r: The Kazerne is a monumental former barracks of the military police, according to its own site. Its page for the autumn 2018 to spring 2019 exhibition, Ongoing Dialogue, says the barracks had been renovated with great respect for the monument and that Kazerne, Home of Design would open there in December, a place where guests eat, drink, meet, work and even sleep among museum exhibitions.
The exhibition showed recent work by more than 40 designers, among them Maarten Baas, Studio Drift and Léa Mazy.

The photograph album for the Kazerne, with 23 photographs by Ralph Roelse, is titled Eat Drink Design Softwear For Google. The earlier draft could not say what Softwear was. Kazerne's page answers: Softwear is an installation curated for Google by Lidewij Edelkoort in collaboration with the designer Kiki van Eijk, who made a series of wall hangings from collages of the textiles used in Google's hardware, and it had its debut at the Salone del Mobile in Milan that April and was shown in the Netherlands for the first time at Kazerne.
The page presents it as Edelkoort's confirmation, twenty years after she predicted in 1998 that technology would take an important place in daily living space.

A dark hall with panels on the floor, a children's rug and a pale fabric sculpture, which the earlier draft described, fits an installation about textiles and technology, but I cannot say which photograph shows which object.

blocks.x: Awards that were announced before the week

r: The Dutch Design Awards changed their format in 2018. The organizers asked why anyone should separate nominees from winners and chose several winners per category.
On June 28 they announced 24 winners and said that the work of all category winners would be shown during Dutch Design Week, when an overall Future Award winner would also be announced.
The jury named three themes: circularity, technology and trust.

Winners included MX3D Bridge by Joris Laarman Lab and MX3D, Swapfiets, Het Grootste Museum van Nederland by Museum Catharijneconvent and Fabrique, and three Young Designers, Lisa Konno, Manon van Hoeckel and Olivier van Herpt.

One of the 24 was the People's Pavilion from the year before: the awards gallery lists Bureau SLA and Overtreders W's borrowed-materials building as a 2018 Habitat winner and calls it a building with an ecological footprint of almost zero.

The Public Award went to the MX3D Bridge, the 3D-printed steel bridge for an Amsterdam canal. The Dutch Design Awards announced it on October 28, 2018 and said it won by a narrow majority of the votes cast by visitors, who this year could vote only in the exhibition itself, a change meant to stop the prize from going to whoever promotes best online.
The same announcement calls the exhibition very well attended and gives no number.
I did not find who received the overall Future Award in 2018. The June announcement says it would be announced during DDW, and neither the DDW closing release nor the Public Award item mentions it.

blocks.x: What else the record names

r: The Italian design blogger behind Italianbark visited and wrote on November 13, 2018 about the Sectie-C exhibit 28 Grams of Happiness, curated by Justine Kontou, which had work by Rive Roshan, CC Tapis, Moooi and Studio Roos Meerman, and about Studio Drift's Meadow at Kazerne.
That is one visitor's account in a personal blog, and it overlaps with Kazerne's page on Studio Drift.
IO+ reported the economic survey of 2017, commissioned by DDW from Dynamic Concepts: visitors spent almost 15 million euros in shops and hospitality.
Omroep Brabant, recalling the same 2017 calculation in a 2021 profile, wrote almost 17 million euros of spending, and the survey's media value was 17 million euros.

The numbers fit if the profile mixed spending with media value, which I think is likely but cannot prove. The profile adds that in 2013 a large financial deficit seemed to threaten the event and a guarantee from the municipality kept it alive.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2018 collection of 63 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened six on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.

The Mind the Step album holds 28 photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann and Cleo Goossens. Beyond the panels discussed above, a third photograph shows a lattice model of small wooden frames with white spheres on plinths. No title names it.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 20 photographs and the titles name an ABN hotspot, Brabant Living Lab, Renault and NS. A night panorama dated October 28 and credited to Oscar Vinck shows the square under a deep blue sky, with a geodesic dome and a barrel-roofed pavilion with a Brabant Living Lab sign. The Renault photograph shows a copper-colored pavilion with the Renault logo, which agrees with the March release about the partnership.

The Klokgebouw album holds 29 photographs by Goossens, titled by hall, among them a white wall headed Making Design, Understanding Systems. The Design Academy Eindhoven album holds 92 photographs, and the Dutch Design Awards album 28 by Bollmann.
The awards album fits the new format: the winners' work was on show during the week.

blocks.x: Electric rides, a train interior and a prize for algae

r: DDW's news pages fill in several of the things the photographs can only label. The Renault Design Rides were charged at Sectie-C, where Van der Sijs techniek built one of the largest temporary mobile charging stations in Europe for the nine days: ten charging stations with 40 charging points on a supply of three times 160 amps, 18,000 trips expected, and 45 cars that, for the first time, all drove electrically.

The page explains the choice of site: Sectie-C, four former factories turned into a breeding ground for artists, musicians, craftspeople and designers, has direct connections to the high-capacity grid, a remnant of its industrial past.

The railway company NS, the architects Mecanoo and the office-furniture maker Gispen showed a shared vision of a future train interior at the Ketelhuisplein, where visitors were asked for feedback that would feed into the concept.
This is the likely subject of the NS title in the earlier draft's Ketelhuisplein album, though no photograph I read says so.

The New Material Award 2018, organized by the DOEN Foundation, the Kwadraat Fund and Het Nieuwe Instituut, went to Algae Lab Luma by Studio Klarenbeek & Dros and Atelier LUMA, a bioplastic made from algae, with a cash prize of 15,000 euros, and the Fellowship to Basse Stittgen's Blood Related.
The finalists were on show until October 28.

VPRO's De toekomstbouwers series ended on Saturday evening, October 27, with Lex Hoefsloot winning the 10,000 euro building deposit for Lightyear, a car powered entirely by solar energy, chosen by a jury of Martijn Paulen, the architect Afaina de Jong and Koert van Mensvoort.
On opening day DDW described the week as hosting 300,000 visitors and over 2,600 designers, a standing description that the final count of 355,000 then exceeded.
The page also describes DDW Live, a stage in Hall 1 of the Klokgebouw with talks by young talent, the Talk & Walk show and the Radical Imagination Talks.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The 2017 figure of 335,000 covered DDW and the World Design Event. IO+ and DDW's director treat 2018 as DDW's own growth. No source I opened splits the 2017 figure.
Mind the Step versus TU/e Research.
The earlier draft merged them. The two pages show two exhibitions side by side.

The 2018 announcement says visitors could vote only in the exhibition that year, which it presents as a change meant to keep the prize from following online promotion. A year earlier a DDA announcement had said Sheltersuit won on votes cast online and in the exhibition.
IO+ says almost 15 million euros, Omroep Brabant almost 17 million. IO+ also gives the media value as 17 million. I use 15 million for spending and treat the other as a probable mix-up.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the overall Future Award winner for 2018.
I do not know how many of the 355,000 came from abroad, only that DDW reported a 21 percent rise in international visitors.
I do not know how DDW produced its visitor count, and none of the releases explains it.
I did not open 57 of the 63 Flickr albums, and I did not re-read the six I used.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a theme asks who else will do it, which photograph in the archive would you accept as an answer, and which would you ask to see the receipts for?
