posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2019 set a deadline, and the record shows two pavilions that tried to meet it
posts.subtitle: The If not now, then when? edition read through DDW's releases, its magazine, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2019: two pavilions and a deadline
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2019 (If not now, then when?) from DDW releases, Dutch press and the photo archive, with a correction on the Floriade reuse claim.

r: A festival whose theme is a deadline ought to leave evidence that someone met it, and in 2019 the Ketelhuisplein left a good deal of it in timber and mushroom threads.

I like a theme that can be checked against a building. This essay reads the eighteenth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: twelve items from DDW's press archive and magazine, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards' announcements, a trade site on Floriade, the technical universities' exhibition page and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used five releases and the photographs, and it repeated one claim that turns out to be wrong.

blocks.x: A theme phrased as a deadline

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 19 to Sunday, October 27, 2019, under the theme If not now, then when?

DDW's ambassador release of July 4 called it a continuation of the question who should act, which had been the 2018 theme, and said the aim was to help innovation in ideas, materials and processes scale up.
Paulen, by then called CEO in the release, said designers are capable of changing problems through a fundamental exploration of the questions.
The closing release put it as a call to action to wait no longer.
The release named four ambassadors: Studio Drift (Lonneke Gordijn and Ralph Nauta), the bio-artist Jalila Essaïdi, the design critic Alice Rawsthorn and Stefano Boeri Architetti.

The ambassador texts give each a mission, from interactive installations that move people to bio-based materials, writing that brings in voices from outside design, and architecture that fights the effects of climate change.

blocks.x: The numbers, and a fall of 5,000

r: The closing release reported that DDW19 drew 350,000 visitors, "more professional and international" than before.

IO+ and Omroep Brabant both put that against the previous year's 355,000, a fall of 5,000, and Omroep Brabant added that a spokesperson found it hard to explain: work on the railway at the start of the week and heavy rain were mentioned.
The July release had expected more than 2,600 designers and more than 350,000 visitors, so the final number met the expectation.
The closing release does not give a designer or location count, and I did not find one in the sources I opened.
Omroep Brabant also counted the edition: the eighteenth.
That agrees with DDW's own count of the fourteenth in 2015, and not with the way anniversary editions are spoken of later.

blocks.x: Two pavilions on one square

r: DDW's magazine describes the Ketelhuisplein as one of three main locations the organization curates, with the Klokgebouw and the VEEM, and the one devoted in 2019 to sustainable architecture and society.

The Biobasecamp was designed by Marco Vermeulen. DDW's release of October 20 describes a pavilion built entirely out of trees. Its deck was assembled from modular cross-laminated timber floorboards of 16 by 3.5 meters, and its supporting pillars were poplar trees that had to be cut down along the Den Bosch to Eindhoven motorway for traffic safety.

Omroep Brabant described a wooden roof of a thousand square meters resting on the felled poplars, with forty trees four and a half meters high planted on top, and quoted Vermeulen saying that overnight stays had been planned but the permits did not allow them.
DDW's magazine called it a star-shaped pavilion and an ode to timber construction, and adds that between the trunks visitors could learn about Floriade 2022 and the Brabant Living Lab.
The Growing Pavilion, a few steps away, was conceived by Company New Heroes with the Dutch Design Foundation and partners in construction, science and design.

The release says its mycelium panels were grown in molds in two weeks on hemp residue, with a funnel-shaped cotton roof draining rain into a planter of cattail, a bench of pressed rice straw and a floor of bio-laminate made from pulverized cattail and potato starch glue.
The designers say they did not know how long the mycelium would withstand sun, rain and snow, assumed ten years and called the structure 95 percent circular.
The release also states a carbon account: 16 tons of CO2 emitted in production and 26 tons captured in the grown materials, with 25 tons saved against conventional construction.
Those numbers are the makers' own, quoted by the organizer, and I did not find a published calculation behind them.

blocks.x: A claim that did not hold

r: The earlier draft of this essay repeated DDW's statement that the Biobasecamp "will be reused at the Floriade horticultural show in Amsterdam in 2022".
The magazine also speaks of "Floriade 2022 in Amsterdam and Almere".
The Floriade Expo of 2022 took place in Almere and ran until October 9, 2022, according to MaterialDistrict's report from the site.
That report places the Growing Pavilion in the Mycelium Park there, as a structure that "was also on display during Dutch Design Week 2019".

It does not mention the Biobasecamp. I found no source confirming that the Biobasecamp went to Floriade. The accurate statements are that DDW's release said it was modular and planned for reuse at Floriade, that Floriade 2022 was held in Almere and that the Growing Pavilion appears in Floriade's Mycelium Park.

blocks.x: The program around the square

r: DDW published its themes in stages. The September 24 release opened with food and sustainable farming, robotics and AI, and technology and poetry, and named the Manifestations Festival, curated by Viola van Alphen, with works by more than fifty young artists and recent graduates on human beings and technology.
It also named Cirque du Data by RAUM and Clever Franke, and Homo Sensorium by Baltan Laboratories.

On October 1 a second selection covered mobility, privacy and gender identity, including an Embassy of Mobility on the Ketelhuisplein, an exhibition by Renault of three concept vehicles, and a privacy-friendly smart home called Candle.

A third selection on health, published October 11, announced Frank Kolkman's exhibition Emerging Probe Futures at the Embassy of Health in the Klokgebouw, with students from the Eindhoven University of Technology, ArtEZ and the Design Academy.
The last selection, on October 18, grouped plastic solutions, artificial nature and circularity, and described Leonne Cuppen's exhibition Rethinking Plastic with more than 25 designers and companies.

Design United, the research institute of the three technical universities, used a new title in the Klokgebouw in 2019. Its exhibition page calls it TILT SHIFT: Reframing Futures, invites visitors to the heart of the Klokgebouw, and names Alorah Harman as curator and project lead.
The earlier editions had been called Mind the Step.
The new name explains why the 2019 photographs of the Klokgebouw do not carry that title.

blocks.x: Awards on a different calendar

r: The Dutch Design Awards had their own rhythm. The winners of 2019 were announced on June 12 at a private Award Night, and the work of all nominees was shown in a retrospective exhibition during DDW, where visitors could also vote for the Public Award.

The winners were Gispen's Sett for Product, De Rrusie Suit by Bonne Reijn for Fashion, Lochal by Civic Architects, Braaksma & Roos and Mecanoo for Habitat, OPENRNDR by RNDR for Communication, Re-Source for Design Research, BMX by Clever Franke for Service & Systems, the Puccinimethode of the municipality of Amsterdam for commissioning, and Simone Post as Young Designer, with Frans Bevers receiving the BNO Piet Zwart Prize.
The announcement says 36 committee members chose three nominations per category and a jury of eight committee chairs, led by Ine Frings, chose the winners.
The Keep an Eye Foundation gave Post a grant of 12,000 euros, and each of the two other nominees 9,000 euros.

A visitor vote chose Power Plant by Marjan van Aubel Studio, an energy-neutral greenhouse that uses sunlight to make both electricity and food, as the Public Award winner; it was announced on October 25 after what the announcement calls a neck-and-neck race with Simone Post and Gispen.
The 2019 awards came with a wording of their own, "less, but better", which the announcement uses for the winners' pure way of working.

blocks.x: Embassies, rides and a bench of felled trees

r: The magazine's close-up of the square gives a fuller map. Beside the two pavilions stood an Embassy of Safety in a mirrored pavilion, tied to a What if Lab with the Association of Netherlands Municipalities on the question whether safety is a right, a pavilion of ABN AMRO showing four "game changers" including Adrianus Kundert's Transformer table, and a bench made of tree trunks from the project Stormhout by Atelier NL.
The square was also the starting point of the Renault Design Rides and many tours, and the permanent residents YKSI and Broeinest opened their doors.
The Growing Pavilion held, according to the magazine, Christien Meindertsma's Flax chair and a grass dress by Diana Scherer.
The Embassy of Mobility, an open-air space for the general public, business and government, belongs to the same square.

blocks.x: A king in a former factory

r: On April 5, 2019 King Willem-Alexander visited Sectie-C in Eindhoven with the mayor, John Jorritsma, and Paulen.

DDW's Dutch release says four former factories had been transformed some eight years earlier into studios where more than 200 designers work, and that the king visited the studios of Nacho Carbonell, Vantot, Stop Motion Studio and others.
The week itself then had Sectie-C among its places. The release is the organizer's account of a royal visit and I found no second source for the details.

blocks.x: Recognition from the state

r: About seven months after the week, on June 4, 2020, the Council for Culture advised the Minister of Education, Culture and Science to include the Dutch Design Foundation in the national cultural basic infrastructure from 2021. DDW's release called it the first time a national design festival would be included.
The council, in DDW's summary, praised a year-round program embedded in the region, the combination of a curated and a free-form part of the festival, and quality that it called consistent.
Paulen said the advice rewarded the work of designers and partners over what he called the last 19 years of DDW.
The final decision was left to the minister on Prinsjesdag.
That statement is DDW's own report of the advice, and I did not open the council's text for this essay.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2019 collection of 70 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.

I opened six of the 70 on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. Many 2019 photographs carry only the title Dutch Design Week 2019 and no photographer's name, and I left every one of those out.

In the Klokgebouw album one photograph shows a long wall of green and white panels. One panel is headed Theme and carries a text that begins "We find ourselves in a rather unique place" and ends "If not now, then when?" Beside it, panels headed Ambassadors carry portraits and short texts.
It is the one frame I opened where the theme is stated on a wall.

The BioBaseCamp album holds 43 photographs. In one, taken from above by Oscar Vinck, a wide timber deck on tree-trunk pillars rises over a paved square with a wide staircase at its end. Another shows pillars of unstripped trunks under a flat timber roof and a sign reading Biobasecamp. Max Kneefel's photograph of October 25 shows the stairs at night, lit green. The trunks, the deck and the stairs are visible, and they agree with the release and with the press description.

The Growing Pavilion album holds 8 photographs. The one I chose, by Vinck, looks into a round room whose wall is floor-to-ceiling timber shelving, with a reed planter in the middle and a ceiling of wooden slats that fans out from a lamp. It shows the plan and the timber. It cannot show that any panel is mycelium or how long it took to grow, and the release makes those claims.

The Manifestations album holds 21 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge dated October 22 and 26, and the Domusdela X Drift album holds 13 by Ralph Roelse, titled Shy Light and FlyLight. DDW's closing release says Studio Drift presented Shylight and Flylight in the Domusdela, Materialism at the Kazerne and a project made for DDW19, Materialism: The bag project, at the Van Abbemuseum.
The titles are the only place in the archive where a work is named in the file.

blocks.x: Rides, game changers and a golden thumb

r: The partner Renault's own account of the week, posted on DDW's news page, says over 60,000 visitors used the free ZOE Design Rides, that 35 fully electric cars drove more than 65,000 emission-free kilometers and that the three concept cars EZ-GO, EZ-PRO and EZ-ULTIMO were shown in the Netherlands for the first time at the Klokgebouw, which it says drew almost a hundred thousand visitors.
The cars were charged at one of Europe's largest mobile charging squares, installed this time at the TU/e campus by Van der Sijs techniek en automatisering, where in 2018 it had stood at Sectie-C.
The figures are Renault's, not an independent count, and the page describes the whole event only as drawing several hundred thousand visitors.

On the Ketelhuisplein, ABN AMRO's Game Changers Experience showed four winning designs from ten commissions to reduce the ecological footprint, chosen by a panel of bankers and sustainability experts: Adrianus Kundert's Transformer Table, which reveals new layers as it wears; House of Thol's food-storage container; Jalila Essaidi's candles made from waste fat, with the page citing more than 30 million kilos of fat in Dutch wastewater each year; and a washing machine filter by MarcelvanGalenDesign.

The foundation's What if Lab showed in the Klokgebouw a joint project of five Dutch and five Indonesian designers on sustainable education, biomaterials, clean air and resilient neighborhoods, exhibited at the same time at the Bandung Design Biennale.
After the week the platform for disabled residents of Eindhoven, PGE, gave DDW and the light festival GLOW the Golden Thumb for accessibility in 2019, a year after DDW had received the Silver Thumb.
The criteria included wheelchair routes, signage, parking, toilets and assistance.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: DDW says Amsterdam, the magazine says Amsterdam and Almere, and MaterialDistrict says Almere. The 2022 Floriade took place in Almere, and I use that.
The closing release says 350,000, and the trade sites say it is 5,000 fewer than 2018. Both are consistent.
The Growing Pavilion's figures are the makers' own. I found no published calculation.

Omroep Brabant and DDW's own series count 2019 as the eighteenth. DDW's 2020 statement speaks of 19 years of DDW. That counts years, and the series counts editions, so I do not know how the two reconcile.
Design United calls the 2019 show TILT SHIFT, and the earlier ones Mind the Step.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how DDW counted 350,000, or the number of designers and locations for 2019.
I do not know what happened to the Biobasecamp after the week.
I did not find an independent assessment of the Growing Pavilion's carbon account.
I did not read the 64 Flickr albums I skipped, and I did not re-read the six I used.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a pavilion says it is carbon negative, which number would you want written on the wall next to it, and who would you ask to sign it?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2020 had to learn what intimacy means at a distance, and the record shows how fast it moved
posts.subtitle: The New Intimacy edition read through DDW's releases and magazine, the Dutch Design Awards, Dutch trade press and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2020: The New Intimacy, online
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2020 (The New Intimacy) from DDW releases and the awards: the June plan, the September 30 cancellation and the virtual week.

r: A festival about the new intimacy had to learn, seventeen days before it opened, that nobody would be allowed to stand close to anything, and the record shows how a design week rebuilt itself on a screen in under three weeks.

I like a theme that gets tested by events. This essay reads the nineteenth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten items from DDW's press archive, news and magazine, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement, a trade-press report on the online program and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview, and for this edition nobody could have visited in the usual way. An earlier short draft used four releases, an ambassadors page and the photographs. This one adds the timeline, the numbers and the people.

blocks.x: A timeline in four releases

r: On June 8, 2020 the Dutch Design Foundation announced that DDW would go ahead as a combination of a live and an online festival.

The release said that consultation with the municipality of Eindhoven and the Brabant Southeast Safety Region had confirmed that a DDW with more than 350,000 visitors, large central locations and organized transport was unrealistic.

The live part would be a "studio exhibition model": designers would open studios by appointment to a limited number of professional visitors, with a maximum number of visitors per time slot based on floor space, in categories of 10, 30 and 100, and a daily cap for the city.
The rest would be an improved online platform.
On July 7 DDW announced the theme The New Intimacy for what it called the 19th Dutch Design Week.

The text describes a search for a new equilibrium in a time when Covid-19 is one of the major factors accelerating the exploration of ways of relating to each other and the world, and it says the theme illustrates the uniqueness of the edition, which would manifest itself in intimate physical and extensive online forms.
It also noted that recent easing of national guidelines allowed a larger live component.

On September 30 the mayor of Eindhoven, John Jorritsma, decided that the live version could not take place, on advice of the Safety Region and on the basis of an emergency ordinance issued earlier that week after new national measures.

The release quotes the mayor saying that the images of the overflowing healthcare system in spring were still fresh in his mind, and the director Martijn Paulen saying that canceling with two and a half weeks to go was deeply saddening.
DDW said it had been developing a virtual experience for months, which would now become the main stage.
The closing release of October 25 looked back on a virtual edition.

That sequence is DDW's own account, and it is consistent across the four documents: a hybrid plan in June, a theme in July, a cancellation of the live part in late September, and a virtual week in October.

blocks.x: A recognition arriving in the middle of it

r: Between the June plan and the July theme, on June 4, 2020, the Council for Culture advised the Minister of Education, Culture and Science to include the Dutch Design Foundation in the national cultural basic infrastructure from 2021. DDW's news item called it the first time a national design festival would be included.

The item says the council praised a year-round program embedded in the region, the combination of a curated and a free-form part of the festival, and quality delivered consistently, and that the minister would decide on Prinsjesdag in September.

This is DDW's summary of the advice, and I did not read the council's text. The timing matters for the story: the organization lost its physical festival in the same season in which it gained a place in the national funding structure.

blocks.x: What DDW counted

r: The closing release counts over 1,500 designers, 750 3D Viewing Rooms, 600 events and 400 livestreams by designers, 125 DDW TV programs with 3,500 minutes of content, and 50,000 DDW TV viewers.
It says the festival reached "several hundreds of thousands" through several outlets, mainly professionals, and gives no visitor count.
Paulen said the combination of virtual and live would be the future of DDW and that meeting in real life remains indispensable.

The release also records a virtual visit by the minister of education, culture and science, Ingrid van Engelshoven, and the decision to keep the 750 Viewing Rooms online for ninety days instead of nine.
Two other figures circulated. The trade site IO+ reported on the program before it started and counted more than 450 online events.

The two do not conflict: the earlier number was a preview of the program and the later number is DDW's tally of the week, and neither says how an event was defined. IO+ also gave 355,000 as the 2018 attendance, which is the last full-size comparison the sources offer.

These numbers describe reach and not presence, and the difference matters for a theme about closeness. A livestream can reach a person without putting them in a room, and a 3D Viewing Room can show a stand without anyone walking through it.
The figures say what DDW counted. They do not say what a viewer felt, and the release does not claim to know.

blocks.x: Three ambassadors, announced the year before

r: The 2020 ambassadors were announced at the closing event on October 27, 2019: Lidewij Edelkoort, the designer Sabine Marcelis and Sean Carney, who leads healthcare transformation services at Philips.
The magazine's profile written in the week itself shows how each had to change course.

Edelkoort, with Charlotte Grün, made a traveling library from the private book collection of the graphic designer Anthon Beeke, to open at the Van Abbehuis opposite the Van Abbemuseum and then travel to Dutch libraries.

With the museum's director Charles Esche she curated New Melancholy, an exhibition at the Van Abbemuseum and Kazerne Home of Design that puts museum artworks in dialogue with design objects she has collected, which she described as an offer of new ways of thinking about design and art in times of pandemic.

Marcelis made a three-dimensional digital interaction called Tactility with the technology partners 5GHUB and Dimenco, and worked with a gallery on letting remote visitors control cameras placed in a physical gallery space.
Carney gave a keynote calling on designers to design with purpose in healthcare, and announced the winners of a student design challenge.

blocks.x: A week made of programs

r: DDW's daily guides to the week show what a virtual festival looked like on a timetable. Each day began at 11:00 with a program called For starters, in which the design journalist Jeroen Junte talked with young and familiar names from the design field, and gave a daily wake-up call to the previous day's Dutch Design Awards winner.

The guides list, for a single day, a news program from the Embassy of Health on intimacy, a daily talk show from Design United with design researchers from the Delft, Eindhoven, Twente and Wageningen universities, an Antenna series of ten international graduates from five continents, and the Class of 2020 presentations.

DDW had invited all Dutch design schools to make an exhibition on the theme, and when the physical DDW stopped, five of the participating schools decided to show their physical installations in the schools, filmed.
A talent program of 22 designers, Driving Dutch Design, researched the theme of value in podcasts, articles, a virtual group exhibition and six episodes on DDW TV.

blocks.x: Awards on a screen

r: The Dutch Design Awards presented their 2020 winners from October 17 to 24 in a live show on DDW TV, one category a day at 16:00, according to the awards' own announcement.

The eight winners were The Interceptor by The Ocean Cleanup with Fabrique (Product), Forum Groningen by NL Architects with deMunnik-deJong-Steinhauser (Habitat), DEMO by Studio Dumbar (Communication), Collection 005 by Ninamounah (Fashion), Insectology: Food for Buzz by Matilde Boelhouwer (Design Research), MONNIE by Afdeling Buitengewone Zaken with Garage2020 (Service & Systems), Water as Leverage by the national government (commissioning) and Simon Dogger (Young Designer).
The jury, chaired by Ine Frings, wrote of "doing is the motto" and of designers who take responsibility.
I did not find a Future Award for 2020 in the announcement, and I do not state one.

blocks.x: Where the program touched the ground

r: IO+ highlighted a handful of online projects: Aiki, a soft toy that breathes with a child during medical treatment; the IKEA Virtual Greenhouse; Ilse Kremer's Fabulous Fungi, which uses fungal pigments for textile dye; the Bank of Care, which registers unpaid care work; the app Agora for mental wellness of cancer patients; Manifestations, whose 2020 theme was Monsters; and WatAlsStad, in which five designers made workshops for children to shape a city of the future.
That list is a trade site's selection of an online program, and I did not open the projects' own pages.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2020 collection of 25 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened seven on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.
The Viewing Rooms album holds nine renders at 2560 by 1440 pixels, images of virtual rooms and not photographs of rooms, so I did not use them.
What the archive does hold is photographs made in real halls, so the physical objects existed even when the audience was online.

The New Melancholy album holds 24 photographs by Ralph Roelse, titled for the Van Abbemuseum, Lidewij Edelkoort and Kazerne. They show dark halls hung with pale, weathered curtains, a ring of stacked blocks lit from above, a vase on the floor, hanging pods and a wall of small frames, and no visitor appears in the ones I looked at. The magazine names the exhibition and its curators, so the earlier draft's matching by names is now confirmed.
For an exhibition titled New Melancholy an empty room is a fitting record, and for a theme about intimacy it is an uncomfortable one.

The album for the Dutch Design Awards show, titled Live_Habitat, holds 20 photographs by Jeroen van der Wielen and Oscar Vinck of a television studio with a red set, yellow-fronted desks, a DDA logo screen, presenters and guests at mid distance and a camera operator. The awards' announcement confirms that the show was made for DDW TV.

The Self Design Academy at MU has 27 photographs by van der Wielen, among them round wooden benches facing a projection in a concrete hall. The Piet Hein Eek album has 33 photographs by Max Kneefel. A World Design Embassy on circular and biobased building has 26 photographs, and TAC, the Temporary Art Centre, has 22, among them a wall text that reads VIROPHILIA.

blocks.x: Before June, and the call to designers

r: Before the June plan, DDW's corona update told designers that the foundation was working on physical and virtual scenarios.

It said that, taking national guidelines and 1.5-meter distancing into account, it would be naive to think 350,000 visitors could run free around exhibitions for nine days, and that the aim was a meaningful physical DDW different from earlier editions alongside a digital route.
The update is undated, and it reads as written in spring 2020.

After the July theme, a call for designers said DDW20 would combine a virtual and a live festival, that every approved participant would get a digital space for a virtual 3D exhibition, that a limited number of venues would be coordinated for the live part, and that applications closed on September 1.
That is the program the mayor's decision then cut back to the virtual half.

blocks.x: The universities' research talks

r: Design United held its 2020 edition, Up Close & Personal, from October 19 to 23, one theme a day, as a debate around design research: hybrids, eco-logica, living matter(s), silent power and crisis.
The page lists projects such as Roboat, on autonomous mobility on water for Amsterdam, and a robotic play object for education.
DDW's daily guide gives the show a host, Isolde Hallensleben, and a time of 13:00 to 14:00 each afternoon.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: IO+ counted more than 450 online events in its preview, and DDW counted 600 events at the close. DDW's is the later and the organizer's own tally, and I use it, labeled as DDW's.
The June plan promised a live studio component and the September decision removed it. The 2020 edition was virtual, not hybrid.
The mayor's decision removed the live events around DDW, and the schools' filmed installations show that physical objects still existed in rooms. DDW's own guide is the source for the schools.
There is none. The closing release gives reach and viewers of DDW TV, not visitors.
The theme release calls 2020 the 19th Dutch Design Week, which agrees with the series from 2015 (14th) and 2019 (18th), while the June release speaks of "the last 19 years".

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how many people watched or how many were professionals, because DDW gave no breakdown.
I do not know what the New Melancholy exhibition looked like to a visitor, or whether any visitor saw it in person.
I did not open any of the Viewing Rooms, which may no longer be online after the ninety days DDW promised.
I did not read the 18 Flickr albums I skipped and I did not re-read the seven I used.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival has to rebuild itself in seventeen days, which part of it would you save first, the objects, the meetings or the audience?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2021 borrowed its theme from a lost exhibition, and the record shows what it built instead
posts.subtitle: The Greater Number edition read through DDW's releases, a 1968 Milan exhibition, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2021: The Greater Number
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2021 (The Greater Number) from DDW releases, the 1968 Milan exhibition behind the theme, the awards and the photo archive.

r: A theme called The Greater Number asks for a count, and the record of the 2021 edition gives plenty of numbers and none of the one a reader would ask for first, the number of visitors.

I like a theme that sets a trap for the person writing about it. This essay reads the twentieth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten items from DDW's press archive, a design magazine's guide, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement, a review of a book on a 1968 Milan exhibition and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases and the photographs. This one adds the origin of the theme, the timeline from the April plan to the October close, and the people.

blocks.x: The trap: the one number that is missing

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 16 to Sunday, October 24, 2021.
DDW's announcement of the live plan on April 13 said the organizers hoped to welcome visitors in line with the Covid measures in force and that alternative plans were in place.
The September 21 release said the work was spread over eight areas of Eindhoven.
The closing release of October 24 gives no visitor count, no count of designers and no count of locations.
Its figures are the DDW TV episode a day and the thanks to participants and volunteers.
What numbers exist are expectations. The standard description DDW supplies to event listings said more than 350,000 visitors and more than 2,000 designers in more than 100 locations.
Omroep Brabant quoted Paulen in a 2021 profile saying he did not know how many would come and that growth was not the goal, since DDW wanted to connect good designers with good visitors.

Both are statements made before or during the week, and neither is a count. The reason the closing release stays silent is stated on DDW's press page for facts and figures: the organizers write that more is not better, that constant growth in visitors and participants is not what DDW is about, and that they therefore no longer share exact numbers for each edition, only that a few hundred thousand visitors come each year apart from 2020.
The page is undated, so I cannot say from which edition the policy applies. I also looked for DDW's public annual report for 2021 and could not open it.

blocks.x: A theme with a history

r: The Greater Number is the English form of De Carlo's phrase for the 14th Milan Triennale of 1968. The design magazine Wallpaper explains that the architect Giancarlo De Carlo coined it for that exhibition, which dealt with population growth, advances in science and the gap between Western abundance and poverty.
Wallpaper says student protesters destroyed the exhibition a few days after it opened.

A review of Paola Nicolin's book on the Triennale puts it differently: the opening-day protest ended with eviction on June 8, followed by De Carlo's resignation with the whole executive committee, and the exhibition was seen by almost no one.
I use the book review's account of events, because it rests on archival research. The magazine's one-line version is a fair summary of the outcome and not of the timing.

DDW's own statement uses the phrase for a different purpose. Its April release asks whether, after the corona crisis, we will continue on the road built by economic growth, and answers that change should focus on social values and care for the planet, with "a constant search for a better number", sometimes less, sometimes more but of higher quality, and sometimes simply different.
Four sub-themes grew out of it, on the pandemic, the wellbeing economy, climate and inclusivity and the design field.
The closing release repeated the framing, aiming at designers looking for the right balance, towards better and away from simply less or more.
That is the organizer's wording, and I report it as such.

blocks.x: The twentieth edition and its new look

r: DDW called 2021 its twentieth edition and its twentieth anniversary, which agrees with the count of 14th in 2015, 18th in 2019 and 19th in 2020.

The agency thonik, founded by Nikki Gonnissen and Thomas Widdershoven, was chosen without a pitch to design a new visual identity based on continuity and innovation, while Vruchtvlees kept the digital platform.
The release says an independent brand strategist, Roel Stavorinus, would write about the design process as it went along.
After the fully virtual 2020 edition, Paulen said the virtual week could not replace the feeling of a live festival, and that DDW stands for serendipity.

blocks.x: Three ambassadors, three exhibitions

r: The ambassadors, announced on July 16, were the architect Floris Alkemade, Natsai Audrey Chieza of Faber Futures and Christien Meindertsma.

Alkemade, the former Chief Government Architect, presented a labyrinth in the Klokgebouw with the Board of Government Advisors and World Design Embassies, a translation of his essay The Future of the Netherlands: The Art of Changing Direction.
Chieza led Bio Stories at MU, a three-day forum on synthetic biology and what relationships people want with nature.

Meindertsma, with the interactive designers Joel Gethin Lewis and Reza Ali, made the interactive installation Sharing Elements in Microlab, about the matter that connects bodies to the rest of the world.
Meindertsma's earlier book on a pig, the release recalls, showed how many products an average pig ends up in.

blocks.x: Areas, halls and a village

r: The September 21 program release named the pieces. In the Klokgebouw, the technical universities showed work as Design United, and the exhibition It's in our nature explored human relationships with nature, with Emma van der Leest's fungal bio-coating, Living Color's bacteria-dyed textiles and work from Baltan Laboratories and Mediamatic.

On the Ketelhuisplein, Arne Hendriks presented Hara Hachi Bu, a small village where people practice designing, producing and consuming less, and Nieuwe Helden showed The Exploded View, a house built entirely from biobased materials.

The Embassy of Inclusive Society, also on the square, showed Angel-Rose Oedit Doebés, Lydienne Albertoe on the portrayal of people of color in Dutch children's books, Janine Zielman on facial recognition and Karim Aducchi's Social Distancing Fabric, an embroidery project by 200 refugees during the pandemic.
In Microlab Hall, Things that matter included Ineke Hans's injection-molded chair for the label Circuform, which is returned to the store after use.

In Fuutlaan Hall, Cabinet of collaborations, designed and co-curated by Envisions and Studio Rick Tegelaar, set an extra-large conversation table among works by designers and industry, including pairings such as Vincent Schwenk with Microsoft.

The October 14 release adds the Van Abbemuseum program on inclusiveness and geopolitics, Kiki & Joost, a Natlab costume lab by Baltan Laboratories and Mediamatic, and the Design United talk show Up Close & Personal, streamed daily from the Effenaar.
It places the Graduation Show of the Design Academy Eindhoven in the Beursgebouw, with Manifestations, Isola Talents Factory and Class of 21 as young-talent programs.
DDW TV ran an hour every day at 19:00, including the awards.
I leave out the MU project on substance use that the same release describes, because the release gives me nothing I can check beyond its title and framing.

blocks.x: Awards in the week

r: The Dutch Design Awards presented their winners on October 23, 2021.

They were BYBORRE Create for Product, Marker Wadden for Habitat, Stay Sane Stay Safe by Studio Lennarts & De Bruijn with overdeschreef for Communication, Leela by The Fabricant for Fashion, Affect Lab's community-building project for Design Research, Globalance World by Clever Franke for Data & Interaction, the Circulair Warenhuis for commissioning and Audrey Large as Young Designer, with Hella Jongerius receiving the BNO Piet Zwart Award.
MINI gave The Fabricant an extra prize, a year with an electric car and an ambassador role.
Two of those winners appear in the DDW program: the release lists Het Circulair Warenhuis among the projects in Microlab Hall as DDA-nominated.
The rest of the announcement is the awards' own summary, and I did not read the jury reports.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2021 collection of 36 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened six on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.

The Graduation Show album holds 135 photographs by Cleo Goossens. The one I chose shows a dark hall with a lit table of tall vases and glazed pots and a large film screen behind it, with visitors as silhouettes. The release places the show in the Beursgebouw, and the album titles name no building.

The Bio.Stories album holds 141 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 18. The photograph I chose shows a concrete hall with a long dark ribbon on the floor and a ring of pale wooden stools, with a few people small and far away.
The release attributes the project to Chieza's team.

The Klokgebouw album holds 278 photographs, and two sets inside it are titled Cabinet of Collaborations and Class of 21. A wall in the first set lists 16 pairings of designers and companies, among them ByBorre with Natuzzi and VVAND with Microsoft, and a sign in the same set reads Location Fuutlaan.
The program release places Cabinet of collaborations in Fuutlaan Hall, which resolves the earlier draft's puzzle about the sign.
A tall close view in the Class of 21 set shows small glass and mesh vessels on a transparent shelf, with no maker named.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 38 photographs, mostly by Kneefel, dated October 16 and 17. Two aerial photographs show small timber houses with moss roofs among crowds. The release says Hara Hachi Bu is a small village on the square, and The Exploded View is a house, so the timber houses fit one of the two, but no title names either, and the magazine's description of Hara Hachi Bu as a circle of eleven sheds favors that reading.
The Manifestations album holds 83 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge dated October 16 and 17, and the Kiki & Joost album 68 under the title Meanwhile.

blocks.x: Voices from the magazine

r: DDW's own magazine ran columns and interviews around the week, and they fill in what the releases leave out.

The design writer Jeroen Junte wrote that The Greater Number translates simply as less is more but is not only about reducing, since more solutions are needed for the climate crisis, privacy violations and inequality.

He described the Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences' project Slowductivity, on slowness, boredom and manual labor, and ArtEZ's Greater Less, Greater More, on mixed reality as a way to reduce consumption, citing an average of 173 items of clothing in Dutch wardrobes.

He described Alkemade's Labyrinth in the Klokgebouw as a corridor system of white canvases with artworks hidden as signposts, ending with Atelier Van Lieshout's Apocalypse and an alternative exit through a work by Constant on the playing human, and Arne Hendriks's Hara Hachi Bu on the Ketelhuisplein as a circle of eleven sheds.
That description supports the earlier draft's reading of the small timber houses in the aerial photographs as Hara Hachi Bu, though no photo title says so.

The 1m2 Collective, formed by Jeffrey Heiligers, Studio Jeroen van Veluw and ST-DUO, who knew each other from the talent program Driving Dutch Design, showed in the Van Abbemuseum a totem of 18 works chosen by five independent jurors and curators, free of participation costs.
Heiligers said the starting question was how inclusive design events are, and that this applied to DDW itself.
That is a critique of the festival published by the festival, and the magazine item says so plainly.

Natsai Audrey Chieza, in a magazine interview, said her Bio.Stories forum related to the sub-theme It's in our nature, and that she had been invited in 2020 to the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Synthetic Biology, which partnered with her studio Faber Futures on the project.

Christien Meindertsma, with the interaction designers Joel Gethin Lewis and Reza Ali, said her project Sharing Elements was about how people are matter themselves and connected to food, earth and products.

The eight World Design Embassies, a program the foundation started five years earlier, included the Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building, whose curator Lucas de Man of Company New Heroes explained The Exploded View on the Ketelhuisplein, and the Embassy of Food, curated by Chloe Rutzerveld.
Company New Heroes is the same collective that made the Growing Pavilion in 2019.

blocks.x: The universities' talk show

r: Design United returned to a five-day format. Its 2021 edition, Up Close & Personal, put a live talk show hosted by Isolde Hallensleben in the Effenaar for five days, one theme a day: entangled ecologies, connected interactions, changing things, embedded designers and evolving methodologies.

The Design United page dates the edition to October 18 to 22 and gives the year as 2022 in its heading, which is a typo for 2021, since the days and the Effenaar broadcast match DDW's October 14, 2021 release.

blocks.x: What changed after the virtual year

r: DDW's "what's new" guide lists the practical differences from earlier editions.

A ticket or wristband gave nine days of access to the paid locations: the Klokgebouw, Things that Matter in Microlab Hall, the Graduation Show in the Beursgebouw, the Van Abbemuseum, Sectie-C, Dutch Invertuals and Cabinet of Collaborations on the Fuutlaan, Kazerne, the New Order of Fashion Lab and the Philips Museum.
Corona testing was in principle not needed at the official exhibition locations, but an entry pass was mandatory for longer stays such as workshops and lectures.

The bus company Hermes sold a day ticket for 5 euros, and the VEEM was no longer a DDW location, replaced by Microlab Hall, while the former Campina factory had become De Caai, home of Manifestations, Foundation We Are and the Embassy of Food.
The TU/e campus was a new location, celebrating the university's 65th anniversary under the name Heroes of Change.

The guide to Strijp-S points out the Klokgebouw's Labyrinth, an art installation called Autonomous Tree in which visitors converse with a tree, and the Class of 2021 projects of all academies except the Design Academy Eindhoven.

On the Ketelhuisplein it names Studio Speciaal's Portal, and Hendriks's village, where it says visitors learn that 80 percent is enough, and it places Antigoon and Ralph Roelse, two artists with roots in graffiti, in the basement of the skate park at Area 51.
The guide counts eight areas in the city.

The design sector that DDW served was in a mixed mood. The BNO Sector Monitor 2021, republished by DDW, surveyed designers in the second half of 2020: half expected lower turnover in 2020 than in 2019, about two-fifths expected an improvement in 2021, and about 30 percent of self-employed designers without staff had used the temporary bridging scheme for the self-employed.
The monitor's 2019 figures predate the pandemic.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: DDW writes The Greater Number, and Wallpaper writes The Great Number. De Carlo's 1968 exhibition was the Great Number in Italian, and DDW's form is the one for this edition.
Wallpaper says days after opening, the book review says opening day. I use the review.
None exists in the sources I opened, and DDW's press page says it no longer shares exact numbers per edition. The 350,000 figure is a standing description.
DDW says the twentieth. Omroep Brabant's profile also says twentieth.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how many people visited, how many designers took part or how many locations there were, because the closing release says none of it.
I do not know which of the Ketelhuisplein buildings the aerial photographs show.
I did not read the jury reports of the Dutch Design Awards or DDW's annual report for 2021.
I did not read the 30 Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the six I used.
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival asks for a better number and publishes none, what would you ask it to count?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2022 told designers to get set, and the record shows who was ready
posts.subtitle: The Get Set edition read through DDW's releases and magazine, the Dutch Design Awards, a design critic's tips and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2022: Get Set, in the record
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2022 (Get Set) from DDW releases, the awards and the photo archive: the theme, the area map, the Solar Pavilion and the missing count.

r: A theme that says Get Set is a request to start, and the 2022 record shows a festival that started with a question to its own community before it asked anything of the public.

I like a festival that tells its audience what to do next. This essay reads the twenty-first Dutch Design Week from published sources only: nine items from DDW's press archive and magazine, a trade-press report, a broadcaster's guide, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases, one release about the year before and the photographs. This one adds the context around the theme, the program map, the awards and the question of numbers.

blocks.x: A theme that came out of meetings

r: On June 7, 2022 Miriam van der Lubbe, Creative Head of DDW22, announced the theme in a live Q&A on Instagram with the designer Pete Fung.

The release says the theme signals a shift from preparation to action and crystallized out of several meetings with members of the design community, held earlier in the year to test the temperature and ask how DDW could best relate to the design field.

Van der Lubbe's own explanation was that people must be ready for the challenges, must also get their settings right, forge smart coalitions and, above all, get activated, because doing nothing is no longer an option and not everything will work out as planned.
The closing release gave the theme as Get Set, with the line "We're on a mission".
The edition ran from Saturday, October 22 to Sunday, October 30, 2022, and DDW called it the 21st.
That agrees with the count of 14th in 2015 and 20th in 2021.

blocks.x: The ambassadors' mission

r: The ambassadors, announced on September 5, were the solar designer Marjan van Aubel and the Milan and Rotterdam studio Formafantasma, Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin.
The release says the ambassadors were also asked to bring young talent into their mission, which was new that year.
Van Aubel is co-initiator of the first Solar Biennale, held in September 2022, and its closing piece was the Solar Pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein.
Formafantasma's symposium at Kazerne on Sunday, October 23 investigated, in DDW's words, the possibilities and problems of design in answering crucial questions of ecological and social development.

The Solar Pavilion was designed by V8 Architects and Marjan van Aubel Studio. DDW's magazine describes four steel masts between which a sheet of glass solar panels is stretched, colored panels developed with Kameleon Solar, and a design that is fully circular and uses borrowed standard components to be returned.
The same item describes Sunne Experience in the Klokgebouw, an immersive installation of lights that go through a day cycle with a soundscape based on recordings by NASA.

The earlier draft matched a curved, tiled structure in the drone photographs to this pavilion by form alone. The magazine's description of colored panels supports that match, and I still have no title that names it.

blocks.x: The program map

r: The program release of September 13 listed seven thematic exhibitions, all called Get Set for something, that could be seen only during DDW in the Klokgebouw and on the Ketelhuisplein: Durable Living, The Next Generation, Digital Evolvement, Smart Livability (with the exhibition The New Nature of Living), Creations of Trust, Global Wellbeing and Things that Matter.

It also put the Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show in the Microtuin near the station and Manifestations in the VEEM, Next Nature's RetroFuture in the Evoluon, and the program of World Design Embassies, which it said uses eight embassies to explore complex social challenges.
The release spoke of nine areas of Eindhoven.
The October 19 guide named the areas one by one: Station, Center, Canal, West, Hallenweg, Sectie-C, Strijp T+R and Strijp-S, followed by a group of separate locations under the heading Other.

Eight named areas and one group of locations reconcile the two statements. The guide placed the Dutch Design Awards nominees in Microlab Hall, with the exhibition Things that Matter, and gave Eindhoven Central Station a first appearance as a DDW location.
It also named the official opening party at MYLC on October 22, an Envisions retrospective, Expedition Aequalis by Dutch Invertuals and Fillip Studios' Arabidopsis Symphony on the Wilhelminaplein.

At the Van Abbemuseum, the exhibition The collection is... showed design objects from Lidewij Edelkoort's private collection in ten rooms of the old building alongside contemporary art, with an emphasis on alumni and teachers of the Design Academy Eindhoven.
The museum's program page lists it as on show from October 8 to November 6, 2022 and says a second showing would run at Kazerne until spring 2023.
The program release of September 13 called the roughly 50 works recently acquired.
The page names the curators, Edelkoort and Steven ten Thije.

blocks.x: Numbers: what the closing release says and does not say

r: The closing release of November 3 says DDW22 was "on the level of peak year 2019" for visitor numbers and gives no figure.
Peak year 2019 is a loose phrase: DDW's own closing release for 2019 gave 350,000 visitors, and the trade press reported that this was 5,000 fewer than the 355,000 of 2018.
A broadcaster's headline, which I could read but not the text beneath it, says DDW drew 350,000 visitors and that a new generation of designers had risen.
The standard description DDW supplies to the press, quoted by Innovation Origins that week, was more than 2,600 designers and more than 350,000 visitors across about 120 locations.
Innovation Origins counted 598 exhibitions, from which it selected six.
And DDW's own press page says the organization no longer shares exact numbers for each edition.

So the numbers available are these: a loose comparison from DDW, a headline, a boilerplate description and a count of exhibitions by a reporter. None is an audited count. I use 350,000 only as a media figure, and 598 as one reporter's count of exhibitions.

blocks.x: Awards at night

r: The Dutch Design Awards announced and celebrated their winners at the DDA Award Night on October 27, 2022 during DDW.

The winners were REX by Studio Ineke Hans and Circuform for Product, the Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen by MVRDV for Habitat, CAPS LOCK by Ruben Pater for Communication, The Utopia Ball by Yamuna Forzani for Fashion, Waterschool M4H+ by Studio Makkink & Bey for Design Research, Buycloud by Studio Noa Jansma for Data & Interaction, a campaign by Fonds Slachtofferhulp and Morrow for commissioning, and Cream on Chrome (Martina Huynh and Jonas Althaus) as Young Designer.
The Public Award went to the Kleinkijkacademie by Sjaak Langenberg and Rosé de Beer.
The jury text for the year calls it a time when designers take responsibility and collaborate more.
The guide of October 19 put the nominees in Microlab Hall, so a visitor could see the work that the night would judge.

blocks.x: A broadcaster's view

r: The VPRO's guide, ten tips for the week, opens with Manifestations in the VEEM, curated by Viola van Alphen, and gives the example of the Love Letter Generator, in which a language model writes a love letter, and gURL, a teenage bedroom of 2032.

Its second tip is the Solar Pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein, where Van Aubel argues for what the guide calls solar democracy, a world in which people surround themselves with aesthetic solar technology.
That is a critic's selection and the VPRO's reading of Van Aubel's position, and I report them as such.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2022 collection of albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened five on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.

The Klokgebouw album holds 134 photographs, and the titles split the building into Hal 1 to Hal 4, with dates from September 22 to October 26, 2022. The one I chose, titled Hal 3 and dated October 26, shows a teal bicycle on a black table beside a card reading DO NOT TOUCH. No title names the bicycle, and I cannot say which of the seven thematic exhibitions it belongs to.
A hall name and a date are reliable, and the work on the table is not named.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 190 photographs, and several drone photographs by about.today show a tall, curved structure covered in blue, pink and brown tiles rising over the square, with the Philips clock tower in the background. In a closer aerial photograph three people wave from an opening in it.

The Van Abbemuseum album holds 35 photographs, 13 of them titled for Lidewij Edelkoort and dated October 23, 2022, by Boudewijn Bollmann; in the one I chose, two visitors stand before a wall of framed objects, drawings and small sculptures, with a blue globe hanging in the corner. The museum's page shows the exhibition ran in ten rooms, which makes a wall of framed objects plausible.

The Graduation Show album holds 132 photographs, and a set by about.today is titled Graduation Show Microtuin, which matches the release's location. The one I chose shows a long red banner reading WHO CAN AFFORD TO BE CRITICAL?, a table with papers on the floor and visitors far in the background.
The Embassy of Rethinking Plastic album holds 48 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 22 and 23, with file titles that read YKSI, which is a place and not a project.

blocks.x: What the magazine added

r: The magazine's interview with Creative Head Miriam van der Lubbe and the designer Pete Fung, published June 2, gives her account of the theme: DDW is a platform for the community of designers, companies and organizations, the theme asks designers and citizens to get in the right mindset for enormous challenges such as the climate crisis, the war in Ukraine and inequality, and DDW had held meetings with the design community to learn what its members were working on.
Fung called the phrase poetic, the moment before action, in a field often about grand gestures.

Formafantasma's ambassador project was a symposium called Learning With, which the duo said would not be about them: their way of showing who they are is to present young talents such as their students.

The magazine describes GEO-DESIGN, a two-year master's course at the Design Academy Eindhoven led by Formafantasma, which in 2022 delivered its first graduates, some of whom took part, among them Gudrun Havsteen-Mikkelsen's film on Arctic mining and Ayla Kekhia's amended legal text on border enforcement.
The symposium included the researcher Angela Rui and the Design Museum London senior curator Rebecca Lewin.

The What if Lab, a program of the Dutch Design Foundation that pairs designers with organizations, showed results in the Klokgebouw's second hall, among them Muzus's installation with ReumaNederland on making life with rheumatism experienceable and Totaal Lokaal, a project with the engineering firm Sweco on self-sufficient cities.

The eight World Design Embassies, a program the foundation began five years earlier, included the Embassy of Food, whose curator Chloe Rutzerveld laid out three scenarios for the supermarket of 2050, and an Embassy of Water.
The Dutch Design Awards commissioned a column by the curator Nick Axel, who wrote that the nominees show the future has already arrived and that designers bridge the gap between theory and practice.

blocks.x: The universities in two places

r: Design United split its 2022 edition, Transitions, between a Klokgebouw exhibition on October 22 to 30 and an afternoon program of workshops, debate and project presentations in Microlab on October 24 to 28, 15:00 to 18:00, on five themes: more than human design, futuring, politics of design, entanglements with AI and neo craftsmanships.
The 2022 page counts the Klokgebouw expo as part of the same edition.

blocks.x: The opening night, the leadership change and the Floriade link

r: The grand opening took place at MYLC in De Caai, hosted by Jess Oberlin of PLASMA and the chair Jennifer Muntslag, with Van der Lubbe explaining the theme and the State Secretary for Education, Culture and Science, Gunay Uslu, speaking about giving space to creativity, designers and makers.

Van der Lubbe thanked Martijn Paulen for his dedication, and DDW's earlier announcement explains why: after nine years Paulen stepped down as frontman of Dutch Design Week to concentrate on the foundation's strategic development, including World Design Embassies and What if Labs, and DDW looked for a new creative leader.
Paulen said the government had acknowledged DDW as indispensable for the Dutch creative basic infrastructure.
That sentence is his, and it refers to the Council for Culture's advice of June 2020 that DDW's own news item reported.

The Solar Pavilion has a backstory in DDW's own telling. V8 Architects' co-founder Michiel Raaphorst said Marjan van Aubel called them in May asking for help, that they met three days later with Van der Lubbe and sketched a surface that harvests solar energy and forms part of the environment, that the structure holds about five thousand kilos of solar panels and that more than ten parties worked on it.
Visible connections and wires were left in place on purpose, and an app let visitors have their photo taken from a distance via a QR code.

Earlier in 2022 DDW pointed to its presence at the horticultural exposition Floriade Expo 2022 in Almere, open until October 9: the house The Exploded View: Beyond Building from the 2021 Ketelhuisplein, a biobased pavilion by Next Nature hosting 24 designers, and an art pavilion by Studio Ossidiana.
The page places Floriade Expo 2022 in Almere, where the exposition took place.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The September 13 release says nine, and the October 19 guide lists eight named areas plus Other. Both fit one list.
The program release speaks of approximately 50 works, and the museum's page calls the exhibition The collection is... and gives ten rooms and the dates. The museum's page is the more specific.
DDW's phrase "level of peak year 2019" is loose, and its press page says exact numbers are no longer shared. A broadcaster's headline says 350,000.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how many people came, because DDW says it no longer shares exact numbers.
I do not know which Get Set exhibition the teal bicycle or the red banner belongs to.
I did not read the jury texts of the Dutch Design Awards beyond the announcement.
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the five I used.

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival tells its audience to get set and then stops publishing how many came, what would you look for instead as proof that anyone did?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2023 asked visitors to picture this, and the record shows a festival that sorted itself into missions
posts.subtitle: The Picture This edition read through DDW's releases, a royal visit notice, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2023: Picture This, in the record
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2023 (Picture This) from DDW releases, a royal visit notice and the awards: the missions, PONT, the new management and the missing count.

r: A theme that says Picture This invites the obvious test: what can a photograph of the future actually show, and what does a festival do to help a visitor read one.

I like a festival that gives its visitors an instruction they can check. This essay reads the twenty-second Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten items from DDW's press archive, a notice from the royal house, the Dutch Design Awards' announcements and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used four releases and the photographs. This one adds the program structure, the funding news, the management change and the question of numbers.

blocks.x: An urgent call, and a new way to sort a program

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 21 to Sunday, October 29, 2023, and DDW called it the 22nd.
The theme was announced on May 17 in two live Q&A sessions on Instagram, in which Miriam van der Lubbe, Creative Head of DDW, spoke with the media partners DesignWanted and ArchDaily.
The release calls Picture This an urgent call to face the future scenario that follows if we continue living as we do now, and asks what world we would see in 20, 50 and 100 years.
It adds that designers are experts in formulating and visualizing perspectives and can lead people through a process of change and break through paralysis.

What changed was the structure of the program. DDW's April announcement said it would commit for the coming years to ten program lines, five missions and five design perspectives, and encouraged applicants to link their work to them so the program team could curate matches.
The missions begin with verbs: achieving an equal society, boosting health and well-being, challenging the digital future, creating the living environment and enabling a thriving planet.
The design perspectives are signature and collectible design, speculative and social design, product and craft design, service and innovative design, and independent and critical design.
The September 5 release described them as ten brand-new narratives that guide visitors and designers to find each other.

blocks.x: What the October guide put under each mission

r: The October 4 guide gave examples. Under the equal society it listed, among others, Portray Me by International Creative Women in the center and Dialogues of the Unheard by Fresh Grads at Sectie-C.
Under health it listed Design your MRI Experience (for kids) by Aniek Bartels and the Philips Museum and Objects for Wellbeing by Alissa+Nienke.
Under the digital future it listed Mainframe: Living Technology by Synthetic State and a project on game design by Enversed.
Under the living environment it listed the What if Lab project Rethinking shared space with Sweco and Everyday Paradise, co-curated by Lili Tedde and Lidewij Edelkoort.
Under the planet it listed Icon Re/Outfitted by The Visionary Lab with Vitra and Levi's, and Future > Factory > Furniture, a joint project by furniture makers.

It also described seven World Design Embassies. Among them: the Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building, with Possible Landscapes on a regenerative economy; the Embassy of Food, with The farm of the future; the Embassy of Health, with Health as currency; and the Embassy of Inclusive Society.

The September 5 release added places: the Van Abbemuseum's The space between us, A Bite of Void at Albert van Abbehuis, Manifestations on Strijp-S, Perpetuum Mobile by Kiki & Joost at Canal and Next Nature's Spacefarming at the Evoluon on the future of food for 10 billion people in 2050.

blocks.x: Money and management, off the exhibition floor

r: Two announcements in September show the organization behind the week changing shape. On September 19, DDW said the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science would invest 9 million euros over three years in a program called PONT, The Public Design Practice, which the Dutch Design Foundation would coordinate.
The aim, in the State Secretary's words as quoted, was to involve the creative industry more in societal challenges such as the energy transition and housing.
PONT would officially launch during DDW on October 23.

On September 28 the foundation announced that Katja Pahnke would join Martijn Paulen from November 1 as a second member of the management board, with Paulen responsible for strategy and innovation and Pahnke for general and organizational development.
These are the organizer's announcements, and I did not look for the ministry's own text.

blocks.x: A queen, a forest and the hundred best products

r: Queen Máxima made a working visit on the afternoon of Thursday, October 26.

The royal house's notice says she walked around with Van der Lubbe, exploring the role of AI, reuse of industrial residue, sustainable furniture design and unconventional materials in architecture, and that young international designers presented graduation projects and there was an overview of the hundred best designed products of the past two years.
The notice also says DDW has existed since 2001 and draws about 350,000 visitors a year, and that the queen had visited in 2011 and 2016.
The first statement differs from DDW's own edition count, which makes 2023 the 22nd. If the first edition was in 2001, the count would be 23. I come back to this below.
The Dutch Design Awards announced eight winners on September 22, and the retrospective in the week showed their work.
The jury noted that crossovers made up the majority of entries and wrote about the art of weaving, in the sense of craft and technology flowing together.

The Habitat winner, Bosk, by Arcadia, the municipality of Leeuwarden and Bruno Doedens, was a walking forest of more than a thousand trees that moved through Leeuwarden's center for a hundred days in the summer of 2022, helped by about 4,000 volunteers, according to the awards' gallery.
On Thursday of the week it won the Public Award, announced as the opinion of DDW visitors aligning with the jury.
The closing release and the awards' announcement agree on that.

blocks.x: The closing release and its absences

r: The closing release of October 29 describes designers' "shared mission of bettering ourselves" and thanks the beacons Muzus, Yinka Ilori and Stefan Diez.
It names the new programs of the year: the narratives, the interCHANGES series of co-creation sessions, the Avenue of Fresh Perspectives and PONT.
DDW's press page says the organization no longer shares exact numbers per edition.
The royal house's 350,000 is a yearly description.
I do not state an attendance figure for 2023.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2023 collection of albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened seven on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.

The Evoluon album holds 13 photographs by about.today, dated October 20, 2023. In one, a sign reading SPACE FARMING hangs above a long, thin model of a bridge-like truss, with two visitors leaning over it. That sign matches the September 5 program entry for Spacefarming at the Evoluon. Two photographs show a yellow dome whose side panel reads The Embassy of Food, and inside it a plaque headed Future perspectives says the embassy chose five designers as guides. The October 4 guide names the Embassy of Food and its theme, the farm of the future.

Albert van Abbehuis is a villa, and its photographs show it: floral wallpaper, wooden parquet and stained glass, with mirror-steel and stone objects standing in the rooms. The album holds nine photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann dated October 21, and the file titles name Collective Doh. The program names A Bite of Void at the same address, and I found no source linking Collective Doh to that exhibition.

At Canal, the Kiki & Joost album holds 20 photographs by Nick Bookelaar, dated October 22, one of them of a tall timber hall with pink-lit beams and a lone visitor. The program names Perpetuum Mobile by Kiki & Joost for the location.

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 58 photographs by Cleo Goossens, dated October 21, and many titles name the Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building; a second album for that embassy adds photographs by Max Kneefel of greenhouse pavilions with landscape models on round tables, a flax board and a terracotta tower with plants. That fits Possible Landscapes on a regenerative economy.

The Graduation Show album holds 35 photographs by Goossens, dated October 22 and 29. The Dutch Design Awards album holds 44 photographs by Bookelaar, dated October 21 and taken at MicroLab on Strijp-S.

blocks.x: How the week ran, from the daily guides

r: DDW published a daily guide for each of the nine days, and together they give a calendar that the releases do not.

The guide for Saturday, October 21 listed Archiprix 2023 at the Eindhoven University of Technology, a talk on mobility in 2050 with the Embassy of Mobility, the Baltan Laboratories and Onomatopee event The Body is a Movement at Sectie-C and a Kiki & Joost evening at Canal, with dinners at the Kazerne by the caterer Vaderland as the "DDW at Night" item.
As its "hidden gem" it named Bubble Trouble at Koelhuis, a playground in the former Campina freezer warehouse about the illusion of comfort and safety.

The Grand Opening took place in the skate park at Area 51, hosted by Lynn Zebeda and Cesar Majorana, with a takeover by the collective The New Originals, and the captions name the mayor of Eindhoven, Jeroen Dijsselbloem, among the guests.
Van der Lubbe explained the theme on stage and the three beacons, Stefan Diez, Sanne and Neele Kistemaker of Muzus and Yinka Ilori, stood together.
DDW and the auction house Catawiki ran an online auction of design by exhibiting designers from October 21 to 29.
On Monday, October 23 the guide listed DRIVE 2023 at the Effenaar, a day by CLICKNL and Design United, and the first of the area recap videos, for Strijp-S.
On Tuesday the interCHANGES session on the living environment and the thriving planet ran at the Fifth NRE, and Design United's Dialogues ran at Microlab.

The 1m2 Collective, which had shown in the Van Abbemuseum in 2021, returned with a hall at Sectie-C, again to give starting, self-taught and student designers exposure and to make a statement about the inclusivity of design festivals.
On Thursday, October 26 the Embassy of Inclusive Society held a conference at the Van Abbemuseum, the same afternoon as the queen's visit.

The guide for Saturday, October 28 mentions the former Renault design chief Laurens van den Acker, a DDW ambassador in 2018, giving a talk at the Klokgebouw on the Scenic E-Tech electric car, and Next Nature's Evoluon program on the food dilemma.
It describes the week's work as visions from over 2,000 designers.
The last guide, for Sunday, October 29, promised rain, a last day of everything and the Catawiki auction's closing.

Design United's own account of 2023, Ever-changing Relationships, runs from October 21 to 29, with five days of themed dialogues from Monday, October 23: politics of design, climate futures now, more than human, disentangling AI, design and society, and making matters.

blocks.x: Beacons, a talent podium and a club for missions

r: DDW called the first generation of beacons, Yinka Ilori, Stefan Diez and Muzus, guiding lights, and it published profiles in their own words.

Ilori, a British-Nigerian artist and designer, described his public commission Happy Street in Battersea as his first permanent public commission and said its value lay in its effect on the neighbors.

Diez, who has run his studio DIEZ OFFICE in Munich since 2002, said his work follows the principles of a circular economy, giving the BOA chair as made with at least 75 percent recycled material and AYNO and COSTUME as products made to be taken apart, and said there is no contradiction between good and sustainable design.
Those are the designers' statements about their own work, published by the organizer.

The Secrid Talent Podium placed seven designers a year in the Klokgebouw with coaching and a monetary prize, funded by the card-wallet company Secrid, which says it invests 1 percent of its revenue in projects that serve its mission to shift industry from producing more to producing better and has been a certified B Corp since 2022.

VPRO and DDW broadcast a live program on Sunday, October 22, on the relationship between Dutch design and the throwaway society, with the photographer Kadir van Lohuizen, Christien Meindertsma and a Repair Cafe, free to visitors with a ticket.

On Wednesday, October 25 the foundation launched the Mission Club, a place where companies, governments and other organizations can meet the design community; Paulen opened it saying change is a contact sport between governments, the market and designers.
Earlier in the year, on March 9, DDW was among eleven Eindhoven event organizers that signed the Green Events Deal with the city.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: DDW's April release calls 2023 the 22nd edition, and the royal house says DDW has existed since 2001. A count starting in 2002 gives 22, and a start in 2001 gives 23. DDW's own series is internally consistent from 2015 to 2023, so I use it, and I treat the royal house's year as the founding of the event and not as an edition count.
DDW publishes none. The royal house says about 350,000 a year.
The closing release and the awards' announcement agree that Bosk won.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how many people visited in 2023, because DDW says it does not share exact figures.
I do not know what Collective Doh was or whether it belongs to A Bite of Void.
I did not read the jury reports or the full winners list for the Dutch Design Awards 2023.
I did not open the ministry's own text on PONT.
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the seven I used.
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. When a festival sorts its program into missions, how would you check that a project belongs to the one it claims?
