posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2024 asked what was real, and the record shows eleven things built outdoors to answer
posts.subtitle: The Real Unreal edition read through DDW's releases, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2024: Real Unreal, in the record
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2024 (Real Unreal) from DDW releases and the photo archive: Grand Projects, Mission Days, beacons, a bamboo pavilion and the missing count.

r: A theme called Real Unreal sets a trap for a photo archive, because a photograph of an unreal thing is still a photograph of a real one.

I like a theme that forces a reader to check what a picture can prove. This essay reads the twenty-third Dutch Design Week from published sources only: seven items from DDW's press archive, the program page of one pavilion, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases and five photo albums. This one adds the call for entries, the beacons, the Mission Days, the pavilion's history and the awards' year of reflection.

blocks.x: A theme about several realities

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 19 to Sunday, October 27, 2024.

DDW's June 28 release announced the theme Real Unreal and said it addresses how people find their way among the different realities the world now consists of, and where very diverse perspectives meet.
It says designers explore and question what we accept as truths, and it invites visitors to discover things "so good, it's unreal" and to "see real amazing innovations".
The slogan "don't believe everything you think" closes the release.
The call for entries, opened on April 3, called the edition the 23rd and set the deadline for submissions at June 14.

blocks.x: Open doors for ideas that were too big for a booth

r: The call for entries made a point of inviting all kinds of ideas, with a special Call for Grand Projects that might land at one of Eindhoven's prominent squares.
It also announced a more accessible application process, with tutorial videos and walk-in clinics.

The closing release says the open call for Grand Projects got an amazing response and resulted in eleven outdoor projects that DDW could support, some together with the municipality of Eindhoven, which became the eyecatchers on prominent locations.
I note that the count of eleven comes from the organizer and that I did not find a list of all eleven.

blocks.x: The program, by mission

r: The September 10 program release sorted highlights under five missions, with places. Living environment: Teunland 2.0 by Teun Zwets at Piet Hein Eek on Strijp-R, made from reused waste materials, and the Secrid Talent Podium in the Klokgebouw. Thriving planet: Cooling down the city at the NRE Terrain, a collaboration between designers and nature to tackle urban heat stress with a green spa around a revived oak tree, and Designing Society on the Ketelhuisplein. Digital future: Poetics of Prompting at MU and Pokka at Koelhuis. Health and wellbeing: Processing the Unprocessed at Sectie-C and Sharing Bloemfontein, a walking exhibition in Doornakkers. Equal society: the Trilix Bamboo Pavilion and Temple of Peace on the Ketelhuisplein, the latter described as 80 flags designed by teams of design graduates, artists and refugees.

The release also introduced Mission Days, five themed days from Monday, October 21 to Friday, October 25, with morning sessions, afternoon tours and an evening program called DDW at Night, meant to facilitate encounters between designers and professional visitors.
The closing release says DDW co-created and hosted them with ClickNL and Design United.
One of the days, the Digital Future day, included a Design and AI symposium on Wednesday, October 23 at Natlab.

blocks.x: The beacons

r: DDW calls its guest figures beacons, and the October 3 release introduced three new ones.
Julia Watson of the Lo-TEK Institute, author of a book on indigenous technology, was to lecture at the Van Abbemuseum on Saturday, October 19.
Bas van de Poel, innovation director of Modem, presented projects at the Klokgebouw and gave a keynote at the symposium.
André Doxey, who had joined the LEGO Group that year as head of design, completed the three.

The returning beacons were Muzus, with the interactive installation Meaningful Encounters on the Ketelhuisplein, and Stefan Diez, whose students from the University of Applied Arts in Vienna showed in the group exhibition Class of '24.
The release describes the idea of a beacon as a guiding light that spends the first year in a deep dive into DDW and then develops a project.

blocks.x: A bamboo pavilion with a travel history

r: The program page for the Trilix Bamboo Pavilion, by studio akēka with the Dutch Bamboo Foundation, says it was first built in Uganda, then built again in Brussels for the New European Bauhaus Festival in spring 2024, and was in Eindhoven in its third iteration and its first showing in the Netherlands.
It says most of the bamboo was harvested in Georgia and in the Netherlands and that the structure acts as a shading structure with workshops and discussions.

This is a program text by its makers, and I did not find independent coverage. A bamboo structure had stood on the same square in 2016 as Bambooh Lala, a different project by the agency HeyHeydeHaas, according to a 2016 preview listing and DDW's 2016 closing release.

blocks.x: Awards in a year of reflection

r: The Dutch Design Awards announced in July that 2024 would be a year of reflection: the strategy and processes would be redesigned and a new approach presented early the next year.
In the meantime the exhibition at DDW paired ten earlier Young Designer winners or nominees each with a promising current name, ten plus ten designers, organized under DDW's five missions.
The pairs include Yuta Ikeya spotlighted by Christien Meindertsma and Auke Bleij spotlighted by Bob Hendrikx.
Bleij won the Public Award with Respyre, a concrete that turns urban surfaces into green infrastructure, and received a trophy designed by Meindertsma and printed by her FLOCKS Wobot.
The closing release describes Meindertsma as the first Young Designer to win a Dutch Design Award.

blocks.x: What the closing release says about numbers

r: The closing release of October 29 calls the edition exceptionally high in quality, quotes Creative Head Miriam van der Lubbe saying it may have been the best so far, and announces the next edition as Saturday, October 18 to Sunday, October 26, 2025, with a first Super Early Bird ticket.
DDW's press page says it no longer shares exact numbers per edition.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2024 collection of albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.

I opened five on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. They hold 126 photographs: nine at Piet Hein Eek, 41 at the Klokgebouw, 11 at the NRE terrain, 30 at the Ketelhuisplein and 35 for Designing Society.

Only the NRE photographs name their projects in the file titles. At Piet Hein Eek, the photograph I chose shows a gray chair with an easel for a back, set against a blue block. The file title says Dirk Duif, and the program names Teunland 2.0 at the same site, so the picture and the program entry do not name the same work.

At the NRE terrain, the Cooling-Down-the-City photographs are dated October 23 and credited to Anwyn Howarth. The one I chose shows grasses, flowers and a young tree along the edge of a roof, which fits the program's description of designers working with nature.

At the Ketelhuisplein, a bamboo pavilion with three tall, lit canopies stands on a paved square beside a container marked Drivers of Change. No file title names it, and I match it to the Trilix Bamboo Pavilion by form and place only.

Designing Society has 35 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 19, 20 and 22, which show a glass greenhouse where visitors read boards, listen on headphones and look at a wooden model of a city. The release says the World Design Embassies, Labs and PONT presented together in this exhibition, exploring design as a tool for change.

blocks.x: The ten named Grand Projects

r: The news page on the Grand Projects says an open call was issued in March and that "the final selection of eleven projects" ran from October 19 to 27 on the most prominent squares and locations.

The page names ten: Rayonne by Marion Aeby, a textile installation on the Ketelhuisplein; POND by Nova Innova, a light installation at the Van Abbemuseum lake that translates the water's health into color; Temple of Peace by Peace Seekers, eighty flags made by eighty teams of recent graduates and refugees; We (don't) Want Wind by Noud Sleumer and Nikolai Gillissen; Outpost for Unreal Institutions by Pete Ho Ching Fung and Samein Shamsher at the station square; Inkijkjes in de Energietransitie by Bits of Space and Waag Futurelab; the Eigengrau Pavilion by Zalan Szakacs at Koelhuis; Krijt-je-Rijk by De Reuringdienst on 18 Septemberplein; the Wind Knitting Factory by Studio Merel Karhof on the Nieuwe Emmasingel; and Sex in the City by Noha and Lena Tunkers on the City Hall Square.
That makes ten names against the stated eleven, and I did not find the eleventh.
Designing Society, the Ketelhuisplein greenhouse, had around 40 projects and was free to visit.
It came out of four of the foundation's programs: PONT, World Design Embassies, What if Lab and Maakruimte voor Mooi NL.
Access was planned in: a tactile model at the entrance for visitors with visual impairments, project signs at wheelchair height and a free public tour every hour.
DDW's look back at the exhibition called it the 7th edition of World Design Embassies, with all embassies, PONT and the labs under one roof.

blocks.x: A city's design school, a fire and a newspaper list

r: Not everything that mattered in 2024 happened inside the week. A DDW news item signed by Van der Lubbe, Paulen and Pahnke expressed serious concern about a possible departure of the Design Academy Eindhoven from the city, to Roermond, and argued that creative industries add about one billion euros a year to the region according to municipal research, and that DDW featured in more than 4,000 national and international publications the previous year.
A later DDW news item says it was now certain that the academy would stay in Eindhoven, with the search for a location continuing, quoting the academy's chairman Joseph Grima.
The items carry no date on the page, and the claims about value and publications are the signatories' own.
Shortly before the week DDW reported that the Stroomhuis, an old squatted building and punk venue that had been a DDW location for years, was lost in a fire.
The 2015 releases name the Stroomhuis as the venue of London Calling Part 2 and as a stage for DDW Music.

On October 10 the Dutch newspaper Trouw placed DDW in its Sustainable 100 list at 22nd position as a newcomer, and Van der Lubbe accepted the prize for first place in the Art & Design category at Pakhuis de Zwijger.
The jury chair was quoted saying the list shows the power of working together.

blocks.x: Who paid, who was invited

r: From the 2024 edition DDW selects an annual charity that visitors can support when buying a ticket, and the first was the Dutch Refugee Council, VluchtelingenWerk Nederland; the item gives no amount.

DDW also said it supports Cultuur Inclusief Eindhoven each year, which provided 500 tickets to low-income residents, and partners with Refugee Team Eindhoven and Wasbeer & Pauw so refugees can gain work experience as volunteers.
A ticket was valid for all nine days at the price of a day ticket.
The three Creative Voices, the thing Magazine, Otis Dirk and Benito Walker, were invited to reflect on the program, including through a new DDW TikTok channel.

The Secrid Talent Podium, supported by the Secrid Impact Fund since 2022, again showed product designers, among them Pauline van Dongen's SUNTEX solar fabric, which links to her Umbra Pavilion a year later.
Design United's 2024 edition, Changing Gears, put an expo in the Klokgebouw from October 19 to 27 and dialogues in the Natlab from October 21 to 25 on the five missions.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The call for entries says the 23rd, which agrees with the series (22nd in 2023).
The closing release gives the number, and I did not find a list.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how many people visited, or how many of them came for the Mission Days.
I do not know which photograph shows Teunland 2.0, the Secrid Talent Podium or Temple of Peace.
I do not know the list of the eleven Grand Projects.
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the five I used.
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a theme asks what is real, which of the eleven outdoor projects would you ask to show its working?

posts.title: Dutch Design Week 2025 called design unfinished, and the record shows a festival counting its own birthdays
posts.subtitle: The Past. Present. Possible. edition read through DDW's releases and program pages, an interview with its co-founder, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Design Week 2025: Past. Present. Possible.
posts.description: Dutch Design Week 2025 from DDW releases, program pages and the awards: the anniversary count, two sets of forecasts, Bridging Minds and the Grand Projects.

r: A festival that calls design unfinished has to show unfinished things, and Dutch Design Week 2025 put several of them in the open air while it argued with itself about how old it was.

I like a theme that can be checked against an object. This essay reads the 2025 edition from published sources only: eight items from DDW's press archive, two program pages, an interview with the festival's co-founder, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview of my own. An earlier short draft used five releases, two program pages and the photographs. This one adds the anniversary arithmetic, the awards, the leadership change and the forecasts that do not agree with each other.

blocks.x: A theme that refuses to wrap up

r: The edition ran from Saturday, October 18 to Sunday, October 26, 2025, under the theme Past. Present. Possible.
DDW's release on the theme says the 25th edition is grounded in the belief that design is never finished, and quotes Creative Head Miriam van der Lubbe: "Experiment is the engine of progress."
It says the week presents raw ideas, bold questions and sensory experiments in studios, public squares, repurposed factories and central venues.
The press archive's index dates the release July 8, 2025, and the dateline in the text reads July 10, 2025. I do not know which is the publication date, and I use July.

blocks.x: Counting the birthdays

r: The release calls 2025 the 25th edition and says what began in 2001 as Designers Present grew into an international platform.
The royal house said in 2023 that DDW had existed since 2001.
That does not match the ordinals DDW used in earlier years: the 14th edition in 2015, the 19th in 2020, the 20th and anniversary in 2021, the 22nd in 2023 and the 23rd in 2024.
Those ordinals make 2025 the 24th and put the first edition in 2002, and a 2021 Omroep Brabant profile likewise says the event grew into an international one from 2002.

I can lay out the possibilities and not settle them. If DDW counts a 2001 event as its first edition, then 2025 is the 25th and the earlier ordinals were one short. If it counts from 2002, 2025 is the 24th, and the 2025 release counts a year-zero event. The co-founder, interviewed in a design trade piece, speaks of 25 years and of the 25th edition.
None of the sources I opened explains the shift, and the release with the 2001 detail is the one source for the name Designers Present.
I give the 25th as DDW's own label for the 2025 edition.

blocks.x: Forecasts, and two that disagree

r: No closing figure for 2025 appeared in the sources I opened, and DDW's press page says it no longer shares exact numbers per edition.
What exists are forecasts. The September 18 release said more than 2,500 designers, design schools, ministries and leading brands across 120 venues, with around 350,000 visitors expected.
The September 24 release said work and concepts from 2,000 designers to 350,000 visitors at around 100 locations.
Both are DDW's, six days apart, and they differ by 500 designers and 20 venues. The About DDW page gives more than 2,500 designers and more than 120 locations as the standing description.
I take the larger standing description for the scale and the September 24 numbers as a looser phrasing, and I note that I cannot tell which DDW stands behind.

blocks.x: Eleven installations in public space

r: On August 7 DDW announced eleven large-scale installations by international designers at prominent places in the city, freely accessible, from an open call.

It described five: Econario by Thijs Biersteker, about how political choices ripple through the living environment; the Umbra Pavilion by Pauline van Dongen, a pavilion of solar textile; Factory 5.0 by Aditya Mandlik, in which 10,000 mealworms eat through polystyrene; City At Sea Level by Bahar Orcun, a submerged city; and The Waiting Room by Nanne Brouwer, on privacy in asylum shelters.
Van der Lubbe said the installations bring design to where people already are and invite passers-by to wander, discover and pause.
The September 18 release added that some reach ten meters high.
The 2024 closing release had counted eleven outdoor projects as well, so the number repeats from year to year.

blocks.x: Bridging Minds, and a queen

r: At the Van Abbemuseum the exhibition Bridging Minds, curated by Van der Lubbe as guest curator, showed 100 works across ten rooms of the Old Building.
The program page names the rooms by theme: feeling safe, humans and technology, care and well-being, connection, inclusion, empowerment, innovation, nature, raw materials and freedom.
Named makers include Hella Jongerius, Formafantasma, Jalila Essaidi and Bas Timmer.
An assistant curator, Kirstin Romer, and scouts from the Nieuwe Instituut are credited.
The page says the exhibition was on view from October 4.
Queen Maxima opened the festival on the evening of Thursday, October 16 at Domus Dela, after visiting Bridging Minds, according to the September 24 announcement and the opening release.
The opening release quotes her saying designers have remarkable power to tackle the challenges of our time and are a driving force in the Dutch economy.
It calls the exhibition a selection of 100 designers and artists, while the program page counts 100 works, and I use works.

blocks.x: Class of 25: sixteen or thirty-five

r: The September 18 release says a new generation of talent from 35 leading European design schools was featured in Class of 25.

The program page for the Klokgebouw show lists 16 academies, from the Vilnius Academy of Arts and HKU Utrecht to the Academy of Fine Arts in Gdansk, and says each shows one project at the front of its presentation, together the Avenue of Fresh Perspectives, which capture "the current zeitgeist".
The two numbers do not match, and the Design Academy Eindhoven, which the release names in Class of 25, is not among the 16.
I use 16 for the page and 35 for the release's claim, and I do not know the reason for the gap. The page's own date headers show the 2026 dates, so the listing may have been updated after the week.

blocks.x: Awards, in a new format

r: The Dutch Design Awards presented an Emerging Talent Award on Saturday evening, October 18.

Fifteen nominees were shortlisted, and the jury, chaired by Borre Akkersdijk of BYBORRE, chose three winners: Vera van der Burg, Willem de Haan and Plasticiet (Marten van Middelkoop and Joost Dingemans).
Each received 10,000 euros and a talent development program, funded by the Keep an Eye Foundation.
This continues the 2024 year of reflection, after which the awards have a new approach.
The release describes the awards as founded in 2003.

blocks.x: The people behind the week

r: On August 26, 2025 the foundation announced that Martijn Paulen would step down as managing director on January 1, 2026 after 12.5 years, and that the supervisory board would recruit a successor.

The same year, Van der Lubbe described, in the trade interview, an initiative called Design Development Eindhoven to keep designers able to live and work in a city that expects 70,000 new homes in a decade, and a pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein dedicated to everyone who helped build DDW.
These are her statements, and I did not find a document describing the initiative.

A related announcement of April 3 shows the festival's industrial side. Future > Factory > Furniture, driven by DDW with eight Dutch furniture and textile companies, took its circular-supply-chain project to Milan Design Week.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: DDW's Flickr account carries a 2025 collection of 58 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated.
I opened seven on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version.

The Umbra Pavilion album holds 16 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 18 to 24 in the file titles. In the one I chose, a canopy of pale blue louvered panels rises on a blue mast above curved light-blue benches, with a tower block planted with trees behind it. The photograph shows a public place that people can use. It cannot show a textile generating power, and the release makes that claim.

Factory 5.0 has five photographs by Cleo Goossens, titled with the date October 26. My photograph shows a yellow-orange timber frame shaped like a four-legged animal, in front of a glass facade, carrying rows of white packets, with a visitor reading them. I cannot tell from the picture whether those packets are polystyrene or whether any worms are visible.

The Waiting Room has eight photographs by Kneefel. The one I chose shows a timber room with a patterned cut-out roof, metal bunk beds with blue mattresses and a hanging sheet that begins with the words Once we had dreams, with six visitors at mid distance. That fits a piece about privacy in asylum shelters, and it is a match of subject and not proof of intent.
The album for the Queen's visit holds 45 photographs by Kneefel, all dated October 16, and the Class of 25 album holds 56 photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann titled with the date October 26.
The photograph I chose of the Class of 25 looks down on a long gray platform of small projects with visitors reading them from the edges.

blocks.x: The installations, named

r: A DDW news page of July 7, built with Bureau Binnenstad Eindhoven, lists the Grand Projects for 2025 and again says eleven.

It names ten: City at Sea Level; Econario; The Waiting Room; Factory 5.0; the Institute for Sand Grain Elevation Policy, where visitors scatter a bag of sand as "Sand Grain Distributors"; Rain Café, a rainwater tank that fills with every rainfall and doubles as a meeting place, by Floris Schoonderbeek; SONIC MAZE, an inflatable installation by mesure studio and ultimo intimo; the Umbra Pavilion; the Water Basin Totem by Salu Iwadi Studio, made from recycled construction materials and inspired by West African water basins; and Touching Cellulose, an EduCrafting Pavilion built with visitors from wood, hempcrete and cellulose, guided by TU Delft and TH Koln.
As in 2024, the page states eleven and I count ten.

The page says The Waiting Room is an emergency tent lined with reclaimed wood from bed frames used at a Dutch asylum center in Bleskensgraaf, with bunk beds identical to those in more than 300 reception centers, and made with Planemos, the Netherlands Red Cross and the Eindhoven reception centers Wasbeer and Pauw.
That detail adds to what my photograph shows of blue bunk beds in a timber room.
The page also spells the solar textile of the Umbra Pavilion HELIOTEX where the August release wrote Heliotex.

blocks.x: New this year: hubs, former beacons and a furniture show

r: The foundation introduced HUBS, exhibitions that cluster designers around urgent developments, among them a Young Graduates hub at Fuutlaan 12 and a Textile and Material hub in the Klokgebouw.
Forward Furniture, conceived and curated by Liv Vaisberg at De Caai, showed more than 100 designer studios, each asked to present at least three realized works.

Former beacons returned: Bas van de Poel of Modem presented Dream Recorder, a bedside device that records dreams and plays them back, and a seminar on the design of a design practice; Stefan Diez presented an Exposé on a Circular Design Contract that ties a product's value to its use, durability and return; and the company Hydro showed R100, new work by designers including Keiji Takeuchi, Cecilie Manz, Daniel Rybakken, Sabine Marcelis and Stefan Diez, each limited to a 100-kilometer radius, at the Kazerne.
After the week DDW posted a short thank-you that called the 25th edition a milestone, repeated the dates of DDW 2026, October 17 to 25, and offered no figures.
Design United's 2025 edition, Less Hope, More Action, ran five days of dialogues in the Natlab from October 20 to 24 and an expo in the Klokgebouw.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: DDW says 25th and dates the start to 2001, while its earlier ordinals imply 2002. Unresolved.
Two DDW releases in one week disagree. Unresolved.
The page and the release disagree.
July 8 in the index, July 10 in the text.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how many people visited, since DDW says it does not share exact numbers.
I do not know why the edition count and the founding year do not match.
I do not know the reason for the gap between 16 and 35 schools.
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the seven I used.
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival adds a year to its age, what would you want it to show you to prove that the extra year happened?
